She complained that government critics ignore that progress in favor of using visa revocations of Morena officials as a political weapon.

Sheinbaum said her administration has all but ended thanks to interventions in customs and a series of arrests. She complained that government critics ignore that progress in favor of using visa revocations of Morena officials as a political weapon. 🚫 “There was no list”: Defending legal adviser Luisa María Alcalde, Sheinbaum denied that a “blacklist” of journalists was presented at last Wednesday’s “right of reply” press conference. She said that Alcalde simply showed how stories from reporters such as Ciro Gómez Leyva, Joaquín López Dóriga, Ana Paula Ordorica, Azucena Uresti and Carlos Loret de Mola are amplified on social media to “create an opinion trend.”

Why today’s mañanera matters

The revocation of the U.S. visa of Andrés Manuel López Beltrán, a son of ex-president Andrés Manuel López Obrador and the former secretary of organization for the ruling Morena party, continues to be a major topic in the national conversation. The revocation came after dozens of other Morena officials, including Baja California Governor Marina del Pilar Ávila, were also stripped of their U.S. visas.

At her Tuesday morning press conference, President Claudia Sheinbaum once again offered her opinion on the situation amid calls from the opposition National Action Party (PAN) for López Beltrán to be investigated for alleged involvement in a tax evasion/fuel smuggling scheme known in Mexico as huachicol fiscal.

Today’s mañanera was also significant as Sheinbaum weighed in on another issue that has received significant attention in recent days. That issue is the presentation by presidential legal adviser Luisa María Alcalde of a list of high-profile journalists and media outlets whose critical coverage of the government is said to be amplified online in order to attack the federal government and the “fourth transformation” political movement that Sheinbaum leads.

Sheinbaum reiterates view that revocation of López Beltrán’s US visa was politically motivated

A reporter noted that the Federal Attorney General’s Office said on Monday that it has no proof that would warrant the commencement of an investigation into allegations that López Beltrán is involved in fuel-related crimes. He asked the president whether López Beltrán was ever on authorities’ “radar” for alleged involvement in huachicol fiscal.

“He was not,” Sheinbaum responded.

“And as I mentioned on Friday, from our point of view this is a political issue,” she said, referring to the revocation of López Beltrán’s U.S. visa.

“It’s not related to other issues,” Sheinbaum said.

Rather, she said, it’s a matter of “interference in the decisions of Mexico.”

“… There are other criminals, or alleged criminals, let’s put it that way, where there is no problem [with their U.S. visas],” Sheinbaum said.

“Or there are other politically exposed persons, as they call them, where it’s the other way around — they open the doors to them,” she said.

“I’m not going to name names because I don’t want to get into a controversy,” Sheinbaum said.

Sheinbaum: Opposition is using revocation of López Beltrán’s visa to ‘attack’ the government

Sheinbaum asserted that “as the opposition has no plan for the country,” it uses the revocation of López Beltrán’s visa to “attack the project that we represent.”

“They take away his visa, he decided to make it public with a letter [addressed to U.S. President Donald Trump] and then the barrage of criticism came from the conservative side of politics, from the right, from the pundits, from the media outlets,” she said.

Sheinbaum: Government has ‘practically’ put an end to huachicol fiscal

Sheinbaum asserted that her administration has “practically” put an end to “huachicol fiscal, or the smuggling of fuel.”

“It’s practically over thanks to the interventions that we’ve been carrying out in customs and the arrests that have been made,” she said.

Sheinbaum said that government critics don’t talk about the progress the government has made in combating huachicol fiscal.

Instead, they use revocations of Morena officials’ U.S. visas to attack the government, she reiterated.

“They have the right to do that. Nobody is going to censor them as they claim we will, but it is necessary to point out the work that has been done [to combat huachicol fiscal],” Sheinbaum said.

Sheinbaum defends her top legal adviser amid claims she disseminated a ‘blacklist’ of journalists

A reporter raised remarks made by Luisa María Alcalde at the “right of reply” press conference she held last Wednesday.

🔴La presidenta Claudia Sheinbaum repitió que “no hubo ninguna lista” de periodistas. Explicó que los nombres de periodistas mencionados por Luisa María Alcalde buscaban mostrar cómo las redes sociales y plataformas digitales pueden amplificar información y generar tendencias de… — Azucena Uresti (@azucenau) August 18, 2026

She asked Sheinbaum whether Alcalde, a former interior minister and national president of Morena, had not “directly blamed” certain journalists for initiating an “offensive” against the government because she said that those journalists are the source of anti-government messages that are subsequently amplified on social media, including by bots.

Alcalde faced significant criticism for presenting a so-called “blacklist” of journalists who are said to be opposed to the federal government. In addition, video footage of Sheinbaum saying in 2021 that the drawing up of lists of political adversaries is a practice of McCarthyism and Nazism was widely shared on social media.

On Tuesday morning, Sheinbaum asserted that Alcalde did not in fact present a list at her “right of reply” press conference, a relatively new initiative of the federal government.

“First, there was no list,” she said.

“Names were presented — what Luisa presented … what she showed is the use of digital platforms, of social media, to amplify a piece of news and even create fake news,” Sheinbaum said.

“That’s what she presented,” she said.

Sheinbaum said that Alcalde showed how “a piece of news from these journalists” — among whom were Ciro Gómez Leyva, Joaquín López Dóriga, Ana Paula Ordorica, Azucena Uresti and Carlos Loret de Mola —can be amplified on social media to “create an opinion trend.”

“There are multiple cases of this that we can talk about, many cases,” she said. Narco-government, narco-candidate, narco-president, all that,” Sheinbaum said.

The president went on to say that her government defends the right to free speech.

“Who here has been censored? Give me the name of a journalist we’ve censored,” Sheinbaum said.

“There isn’t one. Tell me the name of a media outlet we’ve censored. There isn’t one,” she said.

World.title: Aeroméxico readies new CDMX-Milan flight for spring 2027
World.content:
Aeroméxico has announced the preparation of a new direct flight between Mexico City and Milan, Italy, scheduled to launch at the start of the 2027 spring season.

The route would connect Mexico City International Airport (AICM) with Milan-Malpensa Airport (MXP), a major air gateway to northern Italy and a strategic hub for business and leisure travelers, as well as for connections to other European destinations.

Milan-Malpensa is located outside the city center but maintains a rail connection to Milano Centrale via the Malpensa Express. The launch of the direct flight would reduce the need for layovers in the United States, Spain, France or the Netherlands, depending on the option chosen by travelers.

The Mexican airline has not yet given information regarding the weekly frequency, days of operation, schedules, introductory fares or flight number, as the project remains subject to the necessary government approvals.

If approved, the new route would make Aeroméxico the only airline in Mexico to connect Mexico City with two destinations in Italy, as the carrier already operates in Italy through its service to Rome-Fiumicino.

“We are very excited to add Milan to our international network, a destination that will allow us to strengthen cultural, commercial, and business ties between Mexico and Italy,” Senior Vice President of Global Sales at Aeroméxico Giancarlo Mulinelli said in a statement.

The new connection could also capitalize on the Italian tourism market’s growing interest in Mexico. According to figures from the Tourism Ministry, air arrivals of visitors residing in Italy last year increased by 13.7% on an annual basis, reaching 102,813 arrivals in the first eleven months of 2025.

The new route will also open up the possibility for travelers from other parts of the country to fly to Milan with a layover in Mexico City, keeping the itinerary within Aeroméxico’s network.

With reports from Aviación 21 and Punto Di Contro

World.title: Inside story: Divers rescue man trapped in unexplored underwater cave
World.content:
On Aug. 4, 2026, two cave divers in Playa del Carmen, Harry Gust and Rosalino Rivera, received a call from the president of Uxpanapa, Veracruz, located deep in the heart of the rugged, dense Selva Zoque, the largest expanse of tropical rain forest remaining in Mexico.

They were tasked with recovering the body of Erasto Crisanto Valdez, a 31-year-old man who had gone spearfishing in a local cenote on July 23 and had not come back out. Divers had searched for him, but had found nothing.

‘Just an easy walk’

“It took us two days to drive all the way to Uxpanapa,” Gust, a professional cave-diving instructor and explorer, told me. “The next morning they told us we only had to walk 900 meters to reach what they were calling a cenote. The local people were really great about helping us carry our gear, but there were lots of surprises.”

According to Gust, he and Rivera had to use a canoe to cross a river that was much larger than they expected.

“The river turned out to be 100 meters wide, and the canoe was a wee bit overloaded,” Gust said. “Another 10 centimeters and we would have been underwater.”

He adds, “What people were calling a cenote was actually a spring pouring out of a hillside, locally known as La Cueva. And we discovered we were now in the state of Oaxaca.”

Despite the long, difficult trek, they eventually made it to their destination.

Rocks as sharp as knives

The cave divers suited up. For safety reasons, Gust went in first while Rivera waited outside.

“The average depth of the cave passage was 6 meters,” Gust told me, “and the visibility was less than a meter. So I went inside, trailing a line behind me, but there was nothing in there that I could tie on to for directional changes.”

Gust said the “almost razor-sharp” rocks on the floor of the passage were anywhere from 30 centimeters to a meter long, and “pointed up like kitchen knives.”

“All you had to do was pull the line across one of them, zigzag twice, and your line is cut through, gone,” Gust said. “Normally you would say this is insane, forget this.”

But then Gust made his call.

“I said, ‘Okay, I’m going for it.’ So I went down the center about 50 meters into the cave and came back out. Couldn’t find anything. I went back low, then high, and next I followed the right wall. Nothing. Finally, I did the left side, and at about 75 meters in, I found a small spare air tank on the floor.”

Gust said he also found a small bag and three rocks for “buoyancy control,” which Gust believes the diver dropped when he ran out of air.

“But the rocks were spread out like breadcrumbs,” Gust said, “showing me which way he went.”

At that point, low on gas and mentally tired, Gust said he “tied off on a small mushroom-shaped rock that had sharp edges on its stem, but not as bad as the others.”

Believing this was a body recovery, he left the cave and returned the next morning.

‘Anybody in here?’

The following day, Gust searched beyond the spare air tank he had found. There, he stumbled upon a D-size flashlight battery lying on the floor of the passage.

“Now I knew I was heading in the right direction,” Gust said. “As I looked up, I saw there was an air space above me, and as I continued forward for 4 meters, I encountered a very strong flow that I couldn’t swim against.”

Gust said he surfaced and noticed a “large dry cave with a creek of water flowing in the middle of it.”

“I muscled myself up out of the water, side-mount tanks and all, and I yelled into the cave in Spanish if there was anybody in there,” Gust said. “And to my utter astonishment, I heard a faint ‘Sí.’”

Gust said he couldn’t believe what was happening.

“I ask him his name, and it’s Erasto — and I say, ‘You’ve been here for two weeks?’ and he said, ‘Yeah.’”

Gust told Crisanto Valdez to hold tight, saying he would be back to complete the rescue.

“‘Your family is waiting outside,’” Gust told the stranded diver.

‘Erasto is alive!’

Gust exited the cave and told the people gathered outside that Crisanto Valdez was alive. As Gust recalled, he had to convince everyone that he was serious.

He told Rivera to suit up so that they could join Crisanto Valdez.

“‘We’re going in so this guy won’t be alone, and if he can move just a little bit, we’re going to take him out,’” Gust told his rescue partner.

“So we went to the dry cave. Rosalino took off his tanks and talked a bit to Erasto, who had been sitting in a niche next to a stream of crystal-clear, drinkable water. He seemed lucid. Then the two of them slowly walked 10 meters to where I was,” Gust said.

While Rivera attached his tanks, Gust talked and joked with Crisanto Valdez to gauge his mental state.

“In his favor was the fact that he knew how to use a diving mask and breathe from a second-stage regulator,” Gust said. “We did a quick checkout, and there he was, breathing the second-stage regulator from Rosalino, supplied by a long hose.”

“Once Erasto was comfortable,” Gust added, “we started the exit.”

Quick exit

Gust said Crisanto Valdez didn’t have any fins, but that didn’t stop a speedy exit.

“We got out in record time,” Gust said. “Maybe five minutes.”

Upon exiting the cave, Crisanto Valdez was nearly blinded by the sunlight. Then, as his adrenaline level dropped, Gust said he “went limp like a baby.”

Sometime later, Gust and Rivera visited Crisanto Valdez in the hospital, where he was recuperating nicely.

Then, still a bit dazed and trying to process what had happened, they started the long drive back to Playa del Carmen.

John Pint has lived near Guadalajara, Jalisco, for more than 30 years and is the author of “A Guide to West Mexico’s Guachimontones and Surrounding Area” and co-author of “Outdoors in Western Mexico.” More of his writing can be found on his website.

World.title: GreenLight will invest US $100M to produce first-of-its-kind RNA biofungicide in Mexico
World.content:
GreenLight Biosciences, founded by Mexican scientist Andrey Zarur, announced on Thursday that it will invest US $100 million to build a biofungicide production plant in the Mexico City metropolitan area.

The firm will use ribonucleic acid (RNA) technology to produce the world’s first RNA biofungicide, which will target specific genes in pests and fungi without harming other organisms or leaving toxic residues in soil, water or crops.

When operational, the completed project will lift Mexico ahead of such markets in the field as the United States, Brazil and the European Union.

“Today, we have set as a goal for our country to create a world-leading biotechnology industry,” said Zarur. Zarur says he sees the project as a major step forward in replacing traditional chemicals and pesticides, many of which are derived from petroleum.

It took over 10 years of research and trials in Mexico and 20 other countries to develop the products to be produced, which were approved by national authorities in a record nine months, according to Zarur.

Economy Minister Marcelo Ebrard said he expects the investment to support the creation of a new value chain in Mexico, centered on knowledge and innovation.

“These ideas, this knowledge, will generate Mexican wealth,” Ebrard said at the investment presentation last week.

The first product developed by GreenLight is an acaricide designed to combat the spider mite, a pest that affects avocados, strawberries and tangerines and causes an estimated 20 billion pesos ($1.17 billion) in damage each year.

Its second product targets a fungus that affects crops such as grapes, strawberries and cucumbers, and causes annual losses of around 10 billion pesos ($587 million). It is already in use on grape crops in Mexico’s well-known wine-producing region of Baja California.

Applying two liters of the product per hectare controls over 99% of the fungus, compared to around 80% using conventional chemical pesticides, according to Zarur.

GreenLight also plans to develop products for strategic non-food crops such as cotton.

The project is expected to support the creation of 500 direct, specialized jobs. With around 11,000 life sciences graduates completing studies in Mexico City each year, the growth of the biotechnology industry will provide these graduates with new job opportunities, according to Arturo Adolfo Palacios Romo, director general of investment attraction at the city’s Economic Development Ministry.

Mexico City is already home to one of the largest clusters of pharmaceutical plants in the region, and the launch of the Tlalpan Innovation District, a US $125-million science and entrepreneurship hub that promotes applied research in health, biotechnology and pharmaceuticals, demonstrates Mexico’s commitment to expanding its biotechnology industry.

With reports from El Economista, La Jornada and México Industry

World.title: Mexico’s women’s flag football team is Olympics-bound after taking bronze at World Championships
World.content:
Mexico’s women’s flag football team secured an invitation to the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics by winning the bronze medal last week at the Flag Football World Championships in Düsseldorf, Germany.

On the men’s side, Canada prevented Mexico from joining their female counterparts in Los Angeles, forcing overtime with 18 seconds remaining in regulation to tie the third-place match at 26-26. The Canadians scored a touchdown and made a 2-point conversion on the opening drive of overtime, then intercepted Mexico on the ensuing possession to secure a 34-26 victory.

In their own bronze medal match Sunday, Mexico’s women — led by captain and quarterback Diana Flores — held off a Great Britain rally from a 13-0 halftime deficit, escaping with a 20-19 win to earn the Olympic bid.

Down by 1, Great Britain, the two-time defending European champs, went for a 2-point conversion with less than 2 minutes remaining, only to be denied when Emily Kemp’s left foot came down out of bounds after catching a pass at the back of the end zone.

Mexico was able to run out the clock thereafter.

“I’m so excited,” Mexico’s Angela Funes Fresan told Olympics.com. “The goal was always to bring home a medal and an Olympic spot, so I’m really happy.”

The Aug. 12-16 World Championships featured men’s and women’s 16-team fields (four groups of four teams each) with two Olympic berths at stake. The U.S. men and women were already assured of automatic bids as the host country.

Both Mexican teams emerged from group play with perfect 3-0 records to advance to the quarterfinals.

There, the women edged Spain 27-26 in dramatic fashion after coughing up a 20-6 lead to fall behind 26-20. For its part, the men easily handled Panama 33-19.

However, both stumbled in the semifinals.

Mexico’s women, ranked No. 1 in the world, were humbled by Canada 20-6, while the men came up just short against World No. 1 USA, 42-40.

Nevertheless, since the U.S. men’s and women’s teams each advanced to the finals, both Mexico squads knew that a victory in their respective third-place game would qualify them for the Los Angeles Games, where Flag Football will make its Olympics debut.

The women did so; the men did not, missing out in heartbreaking fashion.

Mexico’s men still have a chance to qualify for the Olympics via next year’s Flag Football Continental Championships.

With reports from Sports Illustrated, Conade, BBC, SportsNet and ESPN

World.title: CCE: Mexico’s streamlined investment process has spurred US $3.5B in new business
World.content:
Listen to this article

Measures announced by the federal government in May to facilitate investment in Mexico have been “successful,” according to José Medina Mora Icaza, president of the Business Coordinating Council (CCE), an umbrella organization that represents 14 private sector groups.

After a meeting on Friday with government-private sector liaison Altagracia Gómez and Mexico’s Ambassador to the United States Roberto Lazerri, the head of the CCE said that the measures have spurred investments totaling more than US $3.5 billion.

El Embajador @robertolazzeri y Altagracia Gómez #CADERR destacaron la importancia del rol del #CCE en el contexto de la revisión del #TMEC. Coincidieron con el Pdte. @JoseMedinaMora en la importancia de desarrollar proveeduría local para atraer cadenas de suministro a la región y… pic.twitter.com/LT9121UYb4 — Consejo Coordinador Empresarial CCE (@cceoficialmx) August 14, 2026

“Soon we’ll have an announcement because there is already more than $3.5 billion in investments authorized [by the federal government],” Medina Mora told reporters in Mexico City.

He didn’t reveal specific details about the planned investment projects, but said the money would come from Mexican and foreign investors.

Medina Mora’s remarks came around three months after the federal government announced a package of measures within the Plan Mexico framework to unlock and accelerate investments, especially large and strategic ones, by shortening authorization times, simplifying bureaucratic procedures and offering greater regulatory certainty.

“We are accelerating processes, simplifying mechanisms and strengthening legal certainty, because we know that economic development requires clear rules, mutual trust and shared responsibility,” President Claudia Sheinbaum said at an event in Mexico City on May 4.

In accordance with guidelines announced on that date, authorities have a maximum of 30 days to approve or deny strategic projects exceeding 2 billion pesos (US $117 million) within the electronic, pharmaceutical, aerospace, energy or technology industries. For other industries, authorities have a 90-day deadline to respond to proposals.

Medina Mora praises federal government

The CCE chief told reporters that Gómez, head of the government’s business advisory council, acts as a “communication bridge” between the private sector and the Sheinbaum administration.

Medina Mora also said that the federal government’s investment committee is very efficient.

“The investment committee has been very successful. It meets every week,” he said.

“The projects we’ve sent have been approved quickly,” Medina Mora said.

He added that Sheinbaum has “given priority” to the rapid approval of investment projects.

One of 13 goals of Plan Mexico is to reduce the average time between an investment announcement and the execution of a project from 2.6 years to 1 year. Among the other objectives of the ambitious economic initiative are for Mexico to become the 10th largest economy in the world by the end of Sheinbaum’s term in 2030, and to create 1.5 million jobs in Mexico’s specialized manufacturing industry and other “strategic sectors.”

Medina Mora noted that economic growth rebounded in the second quarter of 2026, after a sequential contraction in the first three months of the year. He also said that investment is picking up.

In the first quarter of 2026, Mexico received foreign direct investment totaling a record high of nearly $23.6 billion, an increase of 10.4% compared to the same period of last year.

CCE chief expresses support for fracking

Medina Mora said that the federal government’s openness to large-scale fracking represents an investment opportunity for the private sector.

His remarks came a week after a group of scientists that was tasked with assessing the viability of so-called “sustainable fracking” in Mexico essentially gave its green light to the ongoing evaluation of fracking potential in two basins in northern Mexico, although it recommended against the use of the gas and oil extraction technique in the resource-rich Tampico-Misantla basin.

Medina Mora said that fracking technology “has advanced” and today “takes into account environmental protection and remediation in such a way that there are no [adverse] side effects.”

He said that access to the energy resources that can be obtained via fracking will allow Mexico to have “competitive advantages as a country.” Mexico is currently heavily dependent on the United States for natural gas.

Sheinbaum also asserts that fracking can take place safely and without excessive water use via the employment of new technologies. She said on Aug. 6 that no final decision had been made on large-scale fracking, although it appears very likely that Mexico will move to use the controversial extraction technique in order to boost domestic production of natural gas.

With reports from La Jornada and Infobae

World.title: In latest show of security cooperation, Mexico and US sign drone agreement
World.content:
Mexico and the United States signed a defense agreement on new technologies last week, further strengthening cooperation between the two countries on security matters.

U.S. Ambassador to Mexico Ronald Johnson on Sunday underscored the bilateral cooperation within the declaration of intent that will allow Mexico’s Defense Ministry (Defensa) to acquire drones and counter-unmanned aircraft systems.

Celebrating the agreement and the bilateral commitment to fighting organized crime, Johnson published an image of himself shaking hands with Mexican Security Minister Omar García Harfuch as his Photo of the Week.

“Under the leadership of President Donald Trump and President Claudia Sheinbaum, our cooperation continues to yield results,” he said.

The signatories of the non-binding declaration of intent were García Harfuch, General Héctor Ávila Alcocer and U.S. Army Secretary Daniel Patrick Driscoll. Afterward, Sedena confirmed that no models, quantities, cost or delivery dates have been agreed, and there is no purchase commitment.

In a separate social media post, Johnson said the pact strengthens strategic and operational capabilities, specifically by allowing Mexico’s Defense Ministry “to access the U.S. Army’s digital marketplace to acquire unmanned aerial systems and counter-unmanned aerial systems at competitive costs.”

The agreement follows a December meeting of the U.S.-Mexico Security Implementation Group during which the neighboring countries consented to expand cooperation in dealing with the increased use of drones by criminal organizations.

Also discussed at the meeting was security in the avocado-growing region of Michoacán, where residents have frequently complained about extortion and violence by organized crime cartels.

The situation in that western state prompted the U.S. government to momentarily suspend the avocado trade earlier this month.

With reports from La Jornada, El Financiero and The Rio Times

World.title: Brazil’s Supreme Court Says Cities Cannot Tax a House for Being Big
World.content:
Brazil · Property

Key Facts The ruling It is unconstitutional for a municipal law passed after Constitutional Amendment 29 of 2000 to set the IPTU rate according to the area of a property.

It is unconstitutional for a municipal law passed after Constitutional Amendment 29 of 2000 to set the IPTU rate according to the area of a property. The case ARE 1.593.784, registered as general-repercussion Theme 1.455, with Justice Dias Toffoli as rapporteur.

ARE 1.593.784, registered as general-repercussion Theme 1.455, with Justice Dias Toffoli as rapporteur. The vote Unanimous, in the virtual plenary, concluded on 5 August 2026.

Unanimous, in the virtual plenary, concluded on 5 August 2026. What triggered it A rule in Chapecó, Santa Catarina, charging 1% on properties with a built area of 400 square metres or more.

A rule in Chapecó, Santa Catarina, charging 1% on properties with a built area of 400 square metres or more. Still allowed Higher rates for higher-value property, and different rates by location and by use. Those three criteria are what the 2000 amendment authorised.

Higher rates for higher-value property, and different rates by location and by use. Those three criteria are what the 2000 amendment authorised. Not settled locally Chapecó says the decision has not yet become final in its case.

Size is not wealth, and the court has now said so in a ruling every Brazilian municipality has to follow.

Brazil’s Supreme Court has ruled that a city cannot charge a higher property tax rate simply because a building is large. If you own property in Brazil, this is the kind of decision that changes a bill.

Value, location and use still set the rate. Floor area no longer can. (Photo: Internet Reproduction)

What the court actually decided

The thesis is one sentence: it is unconstitutional for a municipal law passed after Amendment 29 of 2000 to fix the IPTU rate on the basis of the area of the property.

IPTU is Brazil’s municipal property tax. Amendment 29 let cities charge progressive rates, but it named the grounds: the value of the property, where it is, and what it is used for.

Floor area is not on that list. Chapecó argued that a bigger building means more intensive use of the land and therefore justifies a higher rate. The court rejected that.

The reasoning is straightforward. Area is a proxy for wealth, and the Constitution already provides a direct measure of wealth — the assessed value. A city that wants to tax wealth should tax the value.

The rule that started it

Chapecó, a city of about 250,000 in Santa Catarina, passed Complementary Municipal Law 639 in 2018.

It set the IPTU rate at 1% for properties with a built area of 400 square metres or more. Smaller properties paid less.

A taxpayer challenged it, the lower court ordered the rate cut to 0.5% with a refund, and the case travelled up to the Supreme Court, where it was given general repercussion — the status Brazil uses when a ruling should bind every court in the country.

That is why a dispute over one city’s tax table now governs municipal taxation nationwide.

What cities can still do

Quite a lot. Progressive rates by assessed value remain lawful, which is the main tool most municipalities use anyway.

So do different rates by location, which is how cities charge more in central districts, and by use, which is how they separate residential from commercial.

What is gone is the shortcut: a flat rule that says anything over a certain number of square metres pays a higher rate.

Whether you can get money back

Be careful here, because this is where reporting tends to overreach.

In the Chapecó case itself the lower court had already ordered the rate corrected to 0.5% and the overpayment refunded. That is the specific case.

We found no modulation of effects in the Supreme Court decision — nothing limiting how far back it reaches. But that is not the same as a national refund entitlement, and Chapecó has said the decision is not yet final for it.

If you are paying an area-based IPTU rate somewhere, the ruling is binding guidance for every court in the country. Whether you recover past payments is a question for a lawyer and your municipality, not for a headline.

Why it matters if you own property here

General repercussion means the thesis binds every court in Brazil. Municipalities with area-based rules will have to rewrite them.

For foreign owners the practical point is narrower and more useful: check which criterion your IPTU rate is actually set by. If the answer is square metres rather than assessed value, the rule behind your bill is now unconstitutional.

It also tells you something about how Brazilian property taxation works. The country taxes value, location and use, and the Supreme Court has just refused to let cities add a fourth criterion by the back door.

Frequently Asked Questions

What did the Supreme Court decide? That a municipal law passed after Constitutional Amendment 29 of 2000 cannot set the IPTU property tax rate according to the area of a property. The decision was unanimous, concluded on 5 August 2026, with Justice Dias Toffoli as rapporteur. Can cities still charge different rates? Yes. Rates can still vary by the assessed value of the property, by location and by use. Those are the three grounds the 2000 amendment authorised. Floor area is not one of them. Can I get a refund? In the Chapecó case the lower court ordered the rate corrected and the overpayment refunded. There is no reported modulation limiting how far back the ruling reaches, but that is not a general national entitlement — it depends on your municipality and your own case. Does this apply everywhere in Brazil? The thesis carries general repercussion, so it binds every court in the country. Chapecó has said the decision has not yet become final in its own case.

Sources: Rio Times desk research

World.title: Vale Wants Brazil’s Mining Output to Reach US$99 Billion a Year by 2035
World.content:
Brazil · Mining

Key Facts The number Brazil’s annual mineral output could rise from about R$300 billion (US$55 billion) today to as much as R$535 billion (US$99 billion) a year by 2035.

Brazil’s annual mineral output could rise from about R$300 billion (US$55 billion) today to as much as R$535 billion (US$99 billion) a year by 2035. The condition That figure is a ceiling, not a forecast. It assumes 15 proposed measures across four policy agendas are adopted.

That figure is a ceiling, not a forecast. It assumes 15 proposed measures across four policy agendas are adopted. The jobs Total employment supported by the sector — direct, indirect and induced — would go from about 3 million to 5.3 million. That is 2.3 million more than today.

Total employment supported by the sector — direct, indirect and induced — would go from about 3 million to 5.3 million. That is 2.3 million more than today. The tax The study puts the sector’s contribution at R$1.3 trillion (US$241 billion) over 2026 to 2035, against about R$750 billion (about US$139 billion) in the previous decade.

The study puts the sector’s contribution at R$1.3 trillion (US$241 billion) over 2026 to 2035, against about R$750 billion (about US$139 billion) in the previous decade. Who wrote it Vale, with the consultancy Accenture. It was launched at a forum called Destravando o Potencial da Mineração no Brasil, with Vale’s chief executive Gustavo Pimenta taking part.

Vale, with the consultancy Accenture. It was launched at a forum called Destravando o Potencial da Mineração no Brasil, with Vale’s chief executive Gustavo Pimenta taking part. Where it goes The document is to be handed to every candidate for the presidency in the October 2026 election.

This is not a spending plan. It is a list of things Vale wants the next government to do, with a number attached to what happens if it does them.

Vale launched a report in Brasília on Tuesday that puts a figure on what Brazilian mining could be worth in ten years. The number is large and the document is honest about what it is: a set of asks for whoever wins the October election.

The study puts national mineral output at up to R$535 billion (US$99 billion) a year by 2035. (Photo: Internet Reproduction)

What the document actually is

It is worth being precise, because the framing changes what the number means. This is not a Vale investment plan and R$535 billion (US$99 billion) is not Vale’s output target.

It is a sector-wide policy agenda. Vale commissioned it, Accenture produced it, and the audience is the people who will be running Brazil from January.

The company is positioning itself on public policy. That is a normal thing for the largest miner in the country to do in an election year, and it is better read as a negotiating document than as a projection.

The R$300 billion (about US$55 billion) baseline and the 3 million jobs figure are described in the study as current, without a stated base year. Treat them as the study’s own starting point.

Vale S.A., together with its subsidiaries, produces iron ore and nickel in Brazil, Asia, the Middle East, North Africa, Europe, the Americas, and Oceania. The company operates in two segments, Iron Ore Solutions and Vale Base Metals. It extracts, produces, and distributes iron ore, iron ore pellets, briquettes, nickel, copper, other ferrous…

The four agendas

The 15 initiatives sit under four headings: licensing and the fundamentals of mining, integrating the mineral chain, the business and regulatory environment, and shared value creation.

The licensing asks are the concrete ones. They want the permitting process standardised and made predictable, and the agencies that run it — Ibama, Iphan, ICMBio, Funai and the state environment secretariats — strengthened rather than bypassed.

There is a proposal to modernise how mineral titles are managed, and one for the Serviço Geológico do Brasil to partner with private companies on geological mapping.

The rest is about pushing more processing into Brazil rather than exporting raw ore, and about making better use of the CFEM, the royalty that mining pays to the states and municipalities where it operates.

Why the timing is not an accident

Brazil votes in October. A document handed to every presidential candidate two months before the first round is designed to shape a manifesto, not a quarterly report.

Vale has also been under public pressure from the Lula government to invest more and hire more. A study saying the sector could add 2.3 million jobs if the state fixes licensing is an answer to that pressure as much as a proposal.

None of which makes the analysis wrong. It makes it interested, which is a different thing, and readers should hold both facts at once.

The numbers, and what they are not

R$1.3 trillion (US$241 billion) is the sector’s projected tax contribution across 2026 to 2035, against about R$750 billion (about US$139 billion) over the previous decade. That is a doubling, and it is the figure most likely to be quoted at a candidate.

It is worth noting what kind of number this is. It is a projection conditional on a policy programme, produced by the largest company in the industry it describes.

The employment figure has the same shape. Five point three million is the total the sector would support, counting the jobs it creates directly, the jobs at its suppliers, and the jobs created when all those people spend their wages.

Only 2.3 million of those are new. Most Brazilian headlines led with that figure, and it is the more honest one to lead with.

What it means if you are invested in Latin America

Mining permitting is the single largest swing factor in Latin American resource investment, and it is where Chile, Peru and Brazil compete directly.

Chile is running a fiscal argument about copper revenue. Peru has just seen two miners restart stalled projects. Brazil is being asked, in public, to make its permitting predictable.

Whichever country gets there first will take capital from the others. That is the real content of a document like this one.

For anyone holding Brazilian mining equity, the number to watch is not R$535 billion (US$99 billion). It is whether any of the 15 measures appears in a winning candidate’s programme.

What we could not confirm

Vale has not published the report on its own investor site as of Tuesday evening, so the figures here come from the launch coverage rather than from a company release.

Where a number is the study’s own estimate rather than an official statistic, we have said so.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is this a Vale investment plan? No. It is a policy agenda for the Brazilian mining sector as a whole, produced by Vale with Accenture and aimed at the candidates in the October 2026 presidential election. The R$535 billion (US$99 billion) figure is national mineral output, not Vale’s. Is it 2.3 million jobs or 5.3 million? Both, measuring different things. The study puts total employment supported by the sector at up to 5.3 million by 2035, against about 3 million today — an increase of 2.3 million. How much is R$535 billion (US$99 billion) in dollars? About US$99 billion a year at current rates. The current figure of roughly R$300 billion (about US$55 billion) is about US$55 billion. When does Brazil vote? October 2026. That is why the document is being handed to candidates now.

World.title: Brazil Suspends 14 Betting Sites, Including Three From a Company Facing Scrutiny
World.content:
Brazil · Regulation

Key Facts The order The Secretaria de Prêmios e Apostas, the betting regulator inside the finance ministry, issued seven precautionary measures suspending 14 licensed sites belonging to six companies.

The Secretaria de Prêmios e Apostas, the betting regulator inside the finance ministry, issued seven precautionary measures suspending 14 licensed sites belonging to six companies. The penalty R$200,000 (about US$37,000) a day for carrying on regardless.

R$200,000 (about US$37,000) a day for carrying on regardless. The main charge Most were not transmitting operating data to Sigap, the system the regulator uses to watch the market in real time.

Most were not transmitting operating data to Sigap, the system the regulator uses to watch the market in real time. One was different RR Participações was suspended over its corporate paperwork — it did not produce documents on who actually owns it.

RR Participações was suspended over its corporate paperwork — it did not produce documents on who actually owns it. One got two Pixbet received two separate measures: one on data, one for lacking the tools to identify compulsive gamblers.

Pixbet received two separate measures: one on data, one for lacking the tools to identify compulsive gamblers. The dates Signed Thursday 13 August, published Friday 14 August 2026.

The regulator did not accuse these firms of rigging anything. It accused them of not filing, which in a licensed market is the offence that matters.

Brazil’s finance ministry ordered 14 licensed betting sites to stop taking bets. The decisions were signed on Thursday and published on Friday, and the reason in most cases is that the companies were not sending the regulator the data they are required to send.

All fourteen are licensed operators, not the illegal sites the government has been blocking. (Photo: Internet Reproduction)

Who was suspended

Six companies, fourteen domains. ZeroUmBet Plataforma Digital lost zeroum.bet.br, sportvip.bet.br and energia.bet.br.

Pixbet Soluções Tecnológicas lost pix.bet.br, ganhei.bet.br and betdasorte.bet.br. Select Operations lost mma.bet.br, betvip.bet.br and papigames.bet.br.

RR Participações lost multi.bet.br, brx.bet.br and rico.bet.br. Enseada Serviços e Tecnologia lost kbet.bet.br, and Nexus International lost megaposta.bet.br.

These are licensed operators, not the illegal sites the government has been blocking for a year. That is what makes the action notable.

The ZeroUm question, carefully

Three of the suspended domains belong to ZeroUm Bet, a company founded by the lawyer and influencer Deolane Bezerra.

She is not the current owner. Ownership was transferred in December 2024 to José Daniel Carvalho Saturnino, who is the partner-administrator on record.

Bezerra has been in custody since 21 May 2026 on suspicion of laundering money for the PCC criminal organisation, and became a defendant on organised crime and money laundering charges in June. She denies wrongdoing.

There is a further wrinkle. ZeroUmBet was added to the authorised-operator list in April 2025 by court order, after a judge compelled the regulator to include it. The regulator has now suspended a platform it was made to license.

What Sigap is and why not filing is fatal

Sigap is the betting management system. Every licensed operator must feed it operating data so the regulator can see the market as it happens.

Without that feed there is no supervision. An operator that does not file is, from the regulator’s point of view, invisible, and an invisible licensed operator is worse than an unlicensed one.

The legal basis is the 2023 betting law and the ministry’s own 2024 rules on operating conditions. The measures are precautionary — they suspend operations while the sanctioning process runs, rather than cancelling licences outright.

One operator is pushing back

Caio Coimbra, a director at Nexus International, which runs megaposta.bet.br, disputes the finding. He says the transmissions did happen and the files were delivered, and that any gaps arose in processing.

ZeroUm Bet, Select Operations, Enseada and RR Participações had not commented publicly at the time of writing.

We have not been able to find the act published in the official gazette or a notice on the ministry’s own site. Everything here comes from the regulatory and Brazilian business press, and we say so rather than implying a primary document we have not seen.

What a suspension is, and is not

These are precautionary measures. They stop the sites taking bets while the regulator’s sanctioning process runs its course.

They are not licence cancellations, and the companies can in principle satisfy the requirements and return.

The distinction matters for anyone holding the paper of a listed operator. A suspension pending compliance is a very different event from a revocation, even though both stop the revenue on the day.

Why this matters outside Brazil

Brazil licensed its betting market at the start of 2025 after years of grey-market operation, and every other large Latin American market is watching how the enforcement goes.

A regulator that suspends licensed operators for filing failures within eighteen months of opening is signalling that the licence is a supervisory relationship, not a permit you buy once.

For anyone with money in the sector, the compliance cost of a Brazilian licence just became a real number rather than a theoretical one.

Frequently Asked Questions

Are these illegal betting sites? No. All fourteen are licensed operators. That is what makes the suspension significant — the regulator is disciplining companies inside the legal market, not blocking pirates. What did most of them do wrong? They did not send operating data to Sigap, the system the regulator uses to monitor the market. One company, RR Participações, was suspended over documentation on its ownership instead, and Pixbet was also cited for lacking problem-gambling monitoring. What is Deolane Bezerra’s connection? She founded ZeroUm Bet, which operates three of the suspended domains, but transferred ownership in December 2024. She has been in custody since May 2026 on money-laundering suspicion in a separate case and denies wrongdoing. What happens next? The suspensions are precautionary and last while the sanctioning process runs. Operating anyway carries a fine of R$200,000, about US$37,000, a day.

Sources: Rio Times desk research

Africa Intelligence Brief for 18 August: Zambia declares Hichilema with 60.5%, Congo's Ebola outbreak becomes its deadliest, 92 die on Lake Kariba.

Rio Times · Africa Intelligence Brief August 18

Key Facts —Declared in the early hours Zambia’s commission named Hakainde Hichilema president-elect on 18 August, with 2.97 million votes against Brian Mundubile’s 1.86 million. —Two ways to count it That is 60.5% of valid votes against 37.9% for his challenger. An earlier 61.4% figure was a partial count at 192 of 226 constituencies. —Five seats outstanding The chairperson said five of 226 constituencies were untallied but would not materially influence the result. —Observers were critical The European Union mission said election day was calm overall but the broader process ran in an environment that limited fundamental freedoms, on an uneven playing field. —Kenya’s removal contested Former deputy president Rigathi Gachagua has appealed the ruling upholding his impeachment. —Zimbabwe’s worst transport disaster A ferry capsized on Lake Kariba with about 168 aboard. The confirmed toll reached 92 on Tuesday. —Rwanda passes a billion Annual agricultural exports reached about 1.1 billion dollars in the year to June, a first.

Africa Intelligence Brief August 18. (Photo internet reproduction)

The economic news is quieter, cumulative, and considerably better.

Zambia – Declared, and Disputed

Two point nine seven million

Chairperson Mwangala Zaloumis declared Hakainde Hichilema president-elect in the early hours of Tuesday, with 2.97 million votes against Brian Mundubile’s 1.86 million. That is 60.5% of valid votes against 37.9% for his challenger, with twelve other candidates sharing the rest.

Five of 226 constituencies remained untallied at declaration, which she said would not materially influence the outcome. Around five million votes were cast in total.

A seventh attempt and a first

It was Hichilema’s seventh run for the presidency and Mundubile’s first. A Patriotic Front member of parliament, he was adopted as the Tonse Alliance candidate in January and filed his nomination in May on an NRPUP ticket, after court injunctions froze his own party’s leadership. He nonetheless took nearly 38% against a sitting president running on an economic recovery.

Reuters described that as an unexpectedly strong showing, drawing on frustration with lingering hardship despite the turnaround. A recovery visible in the accounts is not always visible in a household.

The Observers – A Playing Field Described as Distorted

Calm on the day, uneven before it

The European Union observation mission said the elections offered voters a competitive choice and that election day was calm overall, but that the broader electoral process took place in an environment that limited fundamental freedoms, on what it called an uneven playing field. Its chief observer is Michael McNamara, a member of the European Parliament, and the mission published its preliminary statement in Lusaka on 15 August.

That is a considered verdict rather than a partisan one. It separates the counting, which appears to have held, from the conditions under which the campaign ran.

The raid nobody disputes happened

The government said eleven opposition officials were detained in a raid on the night of Friday 14 August, the day after the vote and while counting was still under way, at a property where Mundubile was present. He was not arrested. Cabinet Secretary Patrick Kangwa said the operation involved an exchange of fire.

The government accused those detained of holding high-grade military weapons and material for armed insurrection. Mundubile called it an attempt on his life, said colleagues were shot and alleged he was assaulted in custody. Both accounts are claims and we report them as such.

Kenya – A Removal Being Appealed

Back to the Court of Appeal

Former deputy president Rigathi Gachagua has appealed the High Court decision upholding his impeachment, arguing the bench erred in finding his removal could not be reversed despite violations of his constitutional rights. He says the process breached his right to a fair hearing and to meaningful public participation.

He is also challenging the appointment of his successor and wants the Senate’s impeachment resolution declared unconstitutional and void. A separate High Court ruling in Malindi on 7 August held that the election was constitutionally due in 2026 and that the 2027 date is unconstitutional — but suspended that declaration until after the next general election, so the 2027 timetable stands in practice.

And a deal the courts let proceed

In June the Court of Appeal lifted the injunction blocking the sale of a 15% government stake in Safaricom to South Africa’s Vodacom, a deal worth about 1.6 billion dollars. Constitutional challenges are still pending, so it is cleared to proceed rather than settled. Commercial questions are still moving faster through the system than constitutional ones.

The Kenyan temper is litigious rather than resigned, which is a form of institutional health. Everything contested goes to a courtroom.

Zambia’s count held and its campaign conditions did not, according to European observers — a distinction worth more to investors than the winning percentage, because one describes the institution and the other describes the politics.

Uganda – Outlets Closed and Doctors Counted

A shutdown, and a reopening

Uganda’s military ordered Nation Media Group’s outlets shut on 28 June — NTV Uganda, Daily Monitor, Spark TV, KFM and Dembe FM. The communications regulator cleared them to reopen on 29 July and they were back on air by the end of that month.

The order came from the chief of defence forces, not from the regulator, and the regulator was the body that eventually lifted it. That sequence tells you where media policy is actually made in Uganda.

One doctor for every six thousand four hundred

Uganda has 7,871 doctors with active licences to practise in 2026, according to its medical and dental practitioners council. That is roughly one licensed doctor for every 6,400 people.

The central bank held its policy rate at 9.75% last week with inflation described as contained. Monetary stability and clinical capacity are entirely separate achievements.

Rwanda – A Billion Dollars, Quietly

Agricultural exports pass the mark

Rwanda’s annual agricultural exports have surpassed one billion dollars for the first time, reaching about 1.1 billion in the financial year to June — up 24% on the 893 million of the year before, according to the national agricultural export board. It is targeting more than 1.5 billion by 2029.

That is a small landlocked economy building a tradeable sector without minerals or oil. It took a decade and generated almost no headlines.

The unglamorous kind of progress

Kigali is simultaneously containing a Rift Valley fever outbreak in livestock — quarantines from late June, vaccination from mid-July, and a minister saying on 13 August that infections are falling — and planning to double the city’s public transport use within ten years. Neither will move a bond spread this month.

Compounding of this sort is what eventually separates economies. It is also what nobody covers while it is happening.

DR Congo – Past Two Thousand Dead

No vaccine to race to

The Ebola outbreak is now the deadliest in the country’s history. DR Congo’s National Institute of Public Health put the toll at 2,325 deaths from 4,945 confirmed cases as of 15 August, passing the 2,299 killed in the 2018–20 North Kivu epidemic. The World Health Organization’s most recent bulletin, published on 14 August, recorded 4,665 cases and 2,186 deaths as of 12 August.

The WHO said on 10 August that between 60 and 70 per cent of deaths are happening in communities, far from care. The case fatality rate has climbed from about 20% in June to 46% now, and roughly 80% of new cases cannot be traced to a known chain of infection.

And investors bought anyway

The country raised 1.25 billion dollars in its first international bond in April, in two tranches — five-year paper at 8.75% and ten-year at 9.50% — with an order book near five billion. It is the world’s largest cobalt producer and one of the world’s top copper producers.

The bond is from April, not this week. But the pairing stands: capital priced the minerals, not the mortality, and that is a description of what a sovereign bond actually measures.

Zimbabwe – Ninety-Two Dead on Lake Kariba

The deadliest transport disaster in the country’s history

A ferry, the Rida Mbuya Nehanda, capsized on Lake Kariba on the Kariba to Chalala route. The confirmed toll reached 92 on Tuesday, from about 168 people on board, with 67 rescued.

That surpasses the 1991 Nyanga bus crash, which killed 89. It is now the worst transport disaster in Zimbabwe’s recorded history.

A route with no manifest

The figure was confirmed on Tuesday by Marian Chombo, the Mashonaland West provincial affairs minister. The gap between those aboard, those rescued and those confirmed dead has been closing slowly all week.

Lake Kariba carries a great deal of traffic and very little regulation. That combination is the story, and it will outlast the search.

What This Means From Latin America

Separate the count from the campaign

Zambia’s commission suspended a count, resumed it, published constituency by constituency and declared a result within five days. European observers simultaneously judged the campaign conditions to have been distorted.

Both things are true and they describe different institutions. For anyone pricing political risk in a commodity economy, the counting machinery is the part that matters within a quarter.

And watch what compounds

Rwanda passing a billion dollars in agricultural exports took years of steady growth and almost no announcements. Congo raised 1.25 billion dollars in an afternoon on the strength of cobalt.

Latin American economies face the same choice between the mineral and the built sector. Only one of those two paths survives a price cycle.

The Bigger Picture Zambia’s electoral commission declared Hakainde Hichilema president-elect in the early hours of Tuesday with 2.97 million votes against Brian Mundubile’s 1.86 million, 60.5% of valid votes against 37.9%. European Union observers called election day calm overall but said the wider process ran in an environment that limited fundamental freedoms, on an uneven playing field. The pattern repeats across the continent. Kenya’s former deputy president has appealed the ruling upholding his impeachment, Ugandan media outlets were shut by the military for a month before the regulator let them back on air, and the Committee to Protect Journalists reported on 13 August that five detained Ethiopian journalists were pressured to admit involvement in terrorism in exchange for release. The economic news runs the other way and gets less attention. Rwanda’s agricultural exports passed a billion dollars for the first time, up 24% on the year, while Congo, in the middle of its deadliest Ebola outbreak, raised 1.25 billion dollars on cobalt in April.

Africa Intelligence Brief August 18: What We Are Watching

Coming days – Whether Zambia’s opposition mounts a formal legal challenge to the result.

Coming days – The five outstanding constituencies and the eleven detained opposition officials.

Coming months – Kenya’s Court of Appeal on the impeachment, and the contested 2027 election date.

Coming days – Whether Uganda’s newsrooms face further pressure before the next election.

Coming days – The final toll from the Lake Kariba ferry capsize, now 92.

Ongoing – The Congolese Ebola toll, now 2,325 and the deadliest in the country’s history, and the trial of a vaccine licensed for a different strain.

Coming months – Whether Rwanda holds the pace needed for its 1.5 billion dollar export target by 2029.

Go Deeper The full Africa Intelligence Dossier — the interactive risk dashboard, the six people who matter and the downloadable PDF — is updated daily by the Rio Times Intelligence Desk.

More from the Rio Times Intelligence Desk on August 18: the Europe Intelligence Brief, the Asia Intelligence Brief and the USA & Canada Intelligence Brief. For how these stories developed, see the Africa Intelligence Brief for August 17 and the Africa Intelligence Brief for August 15.

Frequently Asked Questions

What was Zambia’s final election result?

Electoral Commission chairperson Mwangala Zaloumis declared Hakainde Hichilema president-elect in the early hours of 18 August, with 2.97 million votes against Brian Mundubile’s 1.86 million, equivalent to 60.5% of valid votes against 37.9% for his challenger. Five of the 226 constituencies remained untallied at declaration, which she said would not materially influence the outcome, and around five million votes were cast in total.

What did international observers say?

The European Union observation mission said the elections offered voters a competitive choice and that election day was calm overall, but that the broader electoral process took place in an environment that limited fundamental freedoms, on an uneven playing field. The government separately said eleven opposition officials were detained in a raid on the night of 14 August, the day after the vote, at a property where Mundubile was present but not arrested, an operation it said involved an exchange of gunfire, with accusations denied by his party.

What is happening in Kenya’s impeachment case?

Former deputy president Rigathi Gachagua has appealed the High Court decision upholding his impeachment, arguing the bench erred in finding his removal could not be reversed despite violations of his constitutional rights, and that the process breached his right to a fair hearing and meaningful public participation. He is also challenging the appointment of his successor and asking the Court of Appeal to declare the Senate’s impeachment resolution unconstitutional and void.

What is notable about Rwanda’s exports?

Rwanda’s annual agricultural exports have surpassed one billion dollars for the first time as its national export board expands into new international markets, with export revenues having quadrupled over the past five years. That is a small landlocked economy building a tradeable sector without relying on minerals or oil, achieved over roughly a decade and with very little international coverage.

USA & Canada Intelligence Brief for 18 August: builders filed more permits and poured less concrete, and a 50% tariff on Canadian goods lands Wednesday.

Rio Times · USA & Canada Intelligence Brief August 18

Key Facts —Single-family building slumped Starts fell 9.9% in July to an annual rate of 808,000, the slowest pace since November 2022 and 15.7% below a year earlier. —The total missed badly All housing starts fell 12.4% to 1.239 million against a forecast of 1.35 million. —But permits rose Building permits increased 5.0% to 1.443 million, with single-family permits up 2.5% to 894,000. —The tariff lands Wednesday Fifty per cent duties on a defined list of Canadian goods — nearly 20 billion dollars a year on the US trade representative’s estimate, about 5% of Canadian imports — take effect on 19 August, with no agreement announced. —Canadian inflation went back up The index rose 3.0% in July from 2.8%, on gasoline and travel tours — but both core measures sat at 2.0%, at the central bank’s target. —Eighteen months of dearer groceries Food from stores rose 3.1%, cooling from 3.9%, but still outpaced the overall index for the eighteenth month running.

USA & Canada Intelligence Brief August 18 — American builders took out more permission to build in July and then built a great deal less.

USA & Canada Intelligence Brief August 18. (Photo internet reproduction)

North of the border, a tariff nobody has managed to stop is now one day away.

Housing – The Sharpest Domestic Number of the Week

Eight hundred and eight thousand

Single-family housing starts fell 9.9% in July to a seasonally adjusted annual rate of 808,000, the Census Bureau reported on Tuesday. That is 15.7% below July of last year and the slowest single-family pace since November 2022.

Total starts including apartments fell 12.4% to 1.239 million, against a forecast of 1.35 million. Economists had expected a mild cooling and received something considerably heavier.

Mortgage rates and unsold inventory

Reuters attributed the fall to higher mortgage costs and a stock of unsold new homes already on the market. The thirty-year fixed rate averaged 6.67% in the week to 13 August, against 6.58% a year earlier. Buyers treat 6% as a threshold rather than a number.

Builders do not stop because they lack demand in the abstract. They stop because the houses they already built have not sold.

Permits – The Contradiction Inside the Same Release

Up five per cent

Building permits rose 5.0% in July to an annual rate of 1.443 million, with single-family permits up 2.5% to 894,000. Permits are the leading indicator and starts are the coincident one.

Builders therefore secured more permission to build while doing less building. That is not a contradiction so much as a description of hesitation.

Keeping the option, declining to use it

A permit costs relatively little and preserves the ability to start when conditions improve. Breaking ground commits labour, materials and financing at today’s rates.

The gap between the two numbers is the clearest read available on American business confidence this month. Companies are ready and unwilling at the same time.

Trade – One Day Left and No Announcement

Fifty per cent, from Wednesday

Duties of 50% are scheduled to take effect on 19 August on a defined list of Canadian goods worth nearly 20 billion dollars a year on the US trade representative’s estimate — about 5% of what Canada sells into the United States — covering products from cement to hockey sticks. Unlike most earlier measures, they apply even to goods that qualify under the North American trade agreement.

Energy, potash, fish and certain critical minerals are excluded, as are the goods already covered by the separate steel, aluminium, copper and vehicle measures. The goods being taxed are the finished ones. The legal route is Section 338 of the Tariff Act of 1930, unused for 96 years and chosen precisely because it sidesteps the trade-agreement exemption that limits the other tariff powers.

Five meetings and no draft

Dominic LeBlanc has met the United States trade representative five times in four weeks, including a virtual session on Sunday and another meeting on Monday. Leaving that meeting he said only that the work is continuing.

Reuters reported the two sides remain far from a draft agreement. Canada’s chief negotiator has told her counterparts that tariffs on Wednesday would represent a cliff that risks halting the talks altogether.

American builders filed more permits and poured less concrete in the same month, and Canadian negotiators held a fifth meeting without a draft — two countries doing the paperwork of confidence while declining to commit to anything expensive.

The Federal Reserve – The Argument Is About Raising

Three dissents, and minutes on Wednesday

Three officials formally dissented at the July meeting in favour of raising rates rather than cutting them. The minutes of that meeting are published on Wednesday.

Markets will read them for how widely the concern about persistent inflation was shared. A committee arguing about increases is a very different animal from one arguing about cuts.

Which is why the housing number matters

Homebuilding is the part of the American economy that responds first and hardest to the cost of money. July’s collapse in starts is what a debate about higher rates looks like at ground level.

The thirty-year government yield traded near 5.31% on Tuesday, reported by Reuters as its highest since 2007. That is the number setting mortgage costs in nine months’ time.

Canada – Prices Went Back Up

Three per cent, on fuel and travel

Statistics Canada reported on Monday that the consumer price index rose 3.0% year over year in July, up from 2.8% in June and a touch above the 2.9% expected. Gasoline prices were 25.7% higher than a year earlier, against 20.5% in June.

Travel tours rose 15.2% and air transportation 12.0%, partly on demand for football tournament trips to American cities. Excluding gasoline the index rose 2.2% for a third consecutive month.

Groceries, for the eighteenth month running

The Bank of Canada’s preferred core measures, however, both sat at 2.0%, up from 1.9% — which is to say at target. The headline move is energy and football travel, not broad price pressure. Food purchased from stores rose 3.1%, cooling from 3.9% in June but still outpacing the all-items index for the eighteenth consecutive month. Fresh fruit rose 6.1%, its largest July monthly move since 2011.

Shelter costs rose only 1.3%, with the cost of replacing a home down 2.1% on the year. The official rate and the shopping trolley have been telling different stories for a year and a half.

The Bank of Canada – Holding, and Watching Wednesday

Core measures stayed near target

The bank’s preferred core measures were steady, with the trimmed measure at 1.9% and the median at 2.0%. That is the reading that lets a central bank look through a fuel-driven headline.

The policy rate has been held at 2.25% through six consecutive decisions. The next one is on 2 September.

The tariff is the bigger variable

Economists at TD noted that with no deal to avert Wednesday’s duties, the trade question remains a clear downside risk to the Canadian economy. Inflation is the smaller of the two problems on the bank’s desk.

Regional differences are wide, with Nova Scotia at 5.0% and Ontario at 2.0%. One country, one policy rate, two and a half points of lived experience.

What This Means From Latin America

The construction cycle is the export cycle

American single-family building at its slowest since 2022 reduces demand for copper, lumber, cement and steel through the autumn. Regional suppliers to the North American construction chain should assume weaker volumes before they assume weaker prices.

The permits number is the counter-argument and it is worth respecting. Approved projects can start quickly once the cost of money moves.

And a tariff that ignores a trade agreement

Wednesday’s duties apply to goods that qualify under the North American agreement, which is the detail that matters most outside Canada. Preferential access has been treated as a starting position rather than a protection.

Mexico is on the same annual review clock, and every regional exporter negotiating market access is watching the precedent. What happens to a treaty partner is the best available guide to what happens to everyone else.

The Bigger Picture American single-family housing starts fell 9.9% in July to 808,000, the slowest pace since November 2022 and 15.7% below a year earlier, with total starts down 12.4% to 1.239 million against a 1.35 million forecast. In the same release, building permits rose 5.0% to 1.443 million. Fifty per cent duties on roughly 20 billion dollars of Canadian goods take effect on Wednesday with no agreement announced, after a fifth meeting between the two countries’ trade chiefs. The duties apply even to goods qualifying under the North American trade agreement. Canadian inflation rose to 3.0% in July on gasoline and travel, with core measures near 2% and groceries above the headline rate for the eighteenth month running. Three American central bankers dissented in July in favour of raising rates, and those minutes arrive Wednesday.

USA & Canada Intelligence Brief August 18: What We Are Watching

19 August – Whether the 50% duties take effect as scheduled, and what Ottawa does within the hour.

19 August – The July Federal Reserve minutes, and how far the case for raising rates extended.

Coming weeks – Whether July’s collapse in starts was a single month or the start of a run.

Coming weeks – Whether the 5% rise in permits converts into ground being broken.

2 September – The Bank of Canada decision, after six consecutive holds at 2.25%.

Coming days – Whether provincial alcohol bans are lifted as part of any settlement.

26 August – The American price index that the long-term yield is reacting to.

Ongoing – The annual review clock on the North American trade agreement.

Frequently Asked Questions

How far did American homebuilding fall in July?

Single-family housing starts fell 9.9% to a seasonally adjusted annual rate of 808,000 in July, 15.7% below the same month last year and the slowest single-family pace since November 2022, while total starts including apartments fell 12.4% to 1.239 million against a forecast of 1.35 million. Reuters attributed the decline to higher mortgage rates and the inventory of unsold new homes already on the market.

Why did building permits rise while starts fell?

Permits rose 5.0% to an annual rate of 1.443 million, with single-family permits up 2.5% to 894,000, in the same Census Bureau release that recorded the fall in starts. Permits are a leading indicator that preserves the option to build at low cost, while breaking ground commits labour, materials and financing at current interest rates, so the gap between the two measures reflects builders keeping their options open rather than using them.

What tariffs take effect on 19 August?

Duties of 50% apply to roughly 20 billion dollars of Canadian goods, covering products from cement to hockey sticks and citing provincial bans on American liquor, Canada’s supply-managed dairy system and quotas on certain American vehicles. Unlike most earlier measures they apply even to goods qualifying under the North American trade agreement, while energy, potash, fish and critical minerals are excluded.

What did Canadian inflation do in July?

The consumer price index rose 3.0% year over year in July, up from 2.8% in June, as gasoline prices rose 25.7% and travel tours 15.2%, while excluding gasoline the index rose 2.2% for a third consecutive month. Groceries rose 3.1%, cooling from 3.9% but outpacing the all-items index for the eighteenth month running, and the Bank of Canada’s core measures stayed near 2% ahead of its 2 September decision.

Sources: Reuters via Investing.com, US Census Bureau, Statistics Canada, Associated Press

Europe Intelligence Brief for 18 August: German expectations jump to 34.2 while ZEW names the Rhine as the risk, and Belgium counts its fire damage.

Now Published in Two Editions Europe Intelligence Brief · Europe Intelligence Dossier You’re reading the Brief — today’s hemisphere at a glance, free, every weekday. The Dossier is the full working document: an editor’s leader, a long-form deep dive on the week’s anchor story, the proprietary Country Risk Dashboard, Trade & Positioning views, data exhibits, and full sources. Subscriber PDF access



Rio Times · Europe Intelligence Brief August 18

Key Facts —German expectations jumped The ZEW barometer rose 7.9 points to 34.2 in August, well above the 30.0 economists had forecast. —A fourth rise in a row It is the highest since February, when the same measure stood at 58.3 — before the Iran war began at the end of that month. —The Rhine is the warning ZEW’s president named record low water on the river as an acute short-term risk even as he described a positive trend. —France’s prime minister was booed Sébastien Lecornu was jeered by residents at Le Porge on Monday, in a commune that lost half its land and 183 houses to July’s Gironde fire. —German harvests will be smaller The farmers’ association puts the grain crop at 41.9 million tonnes, down 7% on last year, after a dry spring and a June heatwave. —Belgium lost a landscape Rain reached Belgium’s largest wildfire since 1911, but the region says the High Fens peat bogs — the country’s only active raised bogs — have suffered an environmental disaster.

Europe Intelligence Brief August 18. (Photo internet reproduction)
