World.title: The delicate (and smoky) art of painting with fire
World.content:
Emily Rose Hastie's journey into the fire-based art form of pyrography started with a cheese board.

A high school teacher from the Gold Coast, Hastie had recently rekindled her childhood love of drawing through a local art collective, focusing on charcoal and toned paper.

Then her mum asked if she could draw a mouse on a new wooden cheese platter she'd bought. But drawing or painting the design would mean the board couldn't be washed.

"I originally used a laser printer at the school to just trial the design, and it was really not that satisfying," says Hastie.

"For me as an artist I was like, 'I can do better'."

Emily Rose Hastie with the self-portrait that saw her selected for Portrait Artist of the Year. (Supplied: ABC TV)

So she visited a hardware store, bought a $30 soldering kit, and gave it a shot.

"It was like I got the soldering iron and this whole world emerged," she says.

Stream Portrait Artist of the Year on ABC iview Talented artists from across Australia compete in a once-in-a-lifetime challenge: capturing iconic celebrities in a race against the clock. Who will be crowned the winner and walk away with a life-changing commission?

Now, Hastie is an established pyrography artist who co-founded her own art studio. In 2021, she had her first solo exhibition, and she entered this year's Archibald Prize with a pyrography portrait of former Greens party leader Christine Milne.

She even appears on the latest season of ABC iview's Portrait Artist of the Year, where she created a pyrography portrait of Danni Minogue in just four hours.

"I love it, I can't even transition back to canvas anymore — it feels strange to me," says Hastie.

" But it was a total happy accident. And I always attribute it to my mum, bless her. "

While Hastie has been exploring this art form for the last few years, it's a practice that goes back thousands.

Ancient songlines of the possum cloak story

Pyrography is an artistic tool practised by cultures all over the world, including by Aboriginal people and Torres Strait Islanders.

While it can be executed on a range of materials, the art form has been long linked with decorating highly valued possum-skin cloaks in south-eastern Australia.

That particular art form was lost to the silence of colonialism for a long time, but younger generations are helping it take on a new life.

Iluka Sax-Williams lives on Wurundjeri country. (Supplied: Iluka Sax-Williams)

Iluka Sax-Williams grew up surrounded by the art of his grandmother, mother, aunts and uncles.

"I've got very fond memories of going to the Koori night markets when I was a child and watching Uncle Mick Harding burning on wood and other materials," says the 26-year-old from the Taungurung people of the Kulin Nation and Zenadth Kes (the Torres Strait Islands).

He was also taught the intricate technique for decorating possum skin cloaks.

"Our ancestors would use these cloaks as a record of one's journey; certain things, depending on your connection to the tribe, would be inscribed on these cloaks," says Sax-Williams.

"As time went on, the cloak would grow with its wearer, and by the time you were ready to rest, you would also be buried with your cloak."

But it's only been in the last 30-odd years that the art form was really revitalised in Aboriginal communities.

Very few cloaks were still in existence, having been destroyed, buried with their owners, or just broken down over time.

Iluka Sax-Williams uses pyrography on many different materials, although he favours kangaroo skin. (Supplied: Iluka Sax-Williams)

But everything changed in 1999 when three women — Aunty Vicki Couzens, Aunty Lee Darroch and Aunty Treahna Hamm — were shown two First Nations cloaks from the late 1800s, which had been stored in the collection of Museum Victoria.

Holding the highly personalised possum skins of their people in the cold storage rooms of the museum had a profound impact on the women.

"It was a call from the ancestors to reawaken the song lines of the possum cloak story, to return the cloaks to our people, to reclaim, regenerate, revitalise and remember," Dr Couzens told the Australian Council for the Arts.

" This is the old people's story and our journey is to carry this vision forward. "

Together with other Gunditjmara people from the western districts of Victoria, Dr Couzens started hosting possum-skin cloak workshops with community, revitalising the practice and connection with the art form.

Iluka Sax-Williams's artwork was displayed on the side of Melbourne trams during Rising Festival. (Supplied: Iluka Sax-Williams)

Inspired from a young age by Dr Couzens' work, Sax-Williams has now built a career for himself with his practice.

A pyrography work on kangaroo skin titled Woora Liwik earned him the RMIT Emerging Artist Award, and was featured on the Rising Melbourne Art Trams. His work will be featured in the upcoming Journey Among Men exhibition at the Koorie Heritage Trust in Naarm/Melbourne.

While he says he was always drawn to "lasers and burning", the cultural link makes him proud.

"These women had to fight hard to get these [cloaks] back into the hands of our people," he says.

"But it's not just that, it's the knowledge as well, and spreading that back to us. That inspires me."

Meditation through burning

Perhaps oddly for an art form that involves a red-hot nib that irreversibly blackens the material it's applied to, both Hastie and Sax-Williams say pyrography calms them.

"I think I'm quite a perfectionist," says Hastie, "and even though I like painting, I love pyrography because I have to commit and be at peace with what I've done."

Emily Rose Hastie uses pyrography to create portraits of people and animals, including Dannii Minogue on Portrait Artist of the Year. (Supplied: Emily Rose Hastie/ABC TV)

And when you're creating intricate portraits with fire, focus is key.

"Every medium has its own gift. I suppose when it comes to pyrography that one's mindfulness."

Hastie says working with all the different types of wood is a challenge, but it also makes every piece completely unique.

"I've always been drawn to nature and there's something so grounding about working with wood," she says.

" You also have the grain, and it's just such a beautiful thing to collaborate with — half the joy is picking a canvas. "

It's also a relatively accessible art form; while there are countless modern tools and toys to explore, Hastie still frequently uses the basic nib she bought from the hardware store.

Actor Luke Carroll wore a kangaroo skin design by Iluka Sax-Williams at the 2026 Logies Awards. (Supplied: Iluka Sax-Williams)

Sax-Williams has experimented with a lot of different materials, too — he favours kangaroo skin, which is larger and thicker than possum.

He runs a lot of pyrography workshops for children and adults, and says his students are always surprised by how pleasant it is.

"I find it very therapeutic; it's a very slow process and it slows me down," he says.

"In this fast-paced world it's kind of hard to get two seconds to yourself, so it's really nice to be able to really zone out, or zone in, and just really dive into it.

" I won't say it's a breath of fresh air, because it's definitely smoky, but it's a lot of fun. "

Teaching is a very important element of Sax-Williams' art practice; his parents ran an Indigenous education consultancy, and raised him to understand the importance of sharing knowledge with others.

"It's part of our culture, it's something that was stripped away from us, and so growing up as a young black fella, we know these are things that we have to pass on to the next generation," he says.

He also teaches the practice to the wider community, and has travelled the world with his art.

"It's really wonderful to be able to share that knowledge, share that culture, but also share that love as well," he says.

"That's what we're all about."

Watch the new season of Portrait Artist of the Year on Sundays at 7.30pm on ABC TV, or any time on ABC iview.

Journey Among Men will be showing from 22 August - 22 November at Koorie Heritage Trust.

World.title: Pivotal Meta trial over social media addiction in children gets underway
World.content:
A coalition of US states suing Meta Platforms over claims Facebook and Instagram were designed in ways that harmed young users' mental health has begun making its case in California federal court, in a trial that could reshape some of the most popular apps on the planet.

Megan O'Neill, a deputy California attorney-general, told the eight-person jury in Oakland, California, that Meta's business model was to "hook the users, hold them for as long as they can, harvest their data, and then hide the truth from the public".

"It worked especially well for kids," she added.

Ms O'Neill told the jury the case was not about taking away Instagram or social media.

"This case is not about whether social media has some benefits for some people. It does," she said.

California Department of Justice Megan O’Neill (left) gave the opening statement for the prosecution in court. (Reuters: Manuel Orbegozo)

California, Colorado, Kentucky and New Jersey are leading a bipartisan group of 29 states suing Meta.

Jurors are expected to issue an advisory verdict, but US District Judge Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers will determine Meta's liability. If she finds Meta liable, Ms Rogers could impose civil penalties and order changes to Facebook and Instagram.

The trial will address claims by the four lead states that Meta designed Facebook and Instagram to addict young children and teenagers, resulting in such harms as anxiety, depression and even suicide, and misled consumers about the platforms' safety.

"Meta needed kids, and it needed to reassure the people who cared about those kids that the kids are safe," Ms O'Neill said.

Jurors will also hear claims by all 29 states that Meta violated federal law by improperly collecting and using the personal data of children while they used its platforms.

Lawyers for Meta are expected to tell the jury that the company has made a huge effort to keep kids safe online. Meta has said it did not make misleading statements about safety, and the states failed to show their residents were harmed.

Meta co-founder and CEO Mark Zuckerberg and Instagram chief Adam Mosseri are expected to testify. The trial is scheduled to last six weeks.

Biggest test yet

Experts have said the trial is the biggest legal test yet of social media's effects on young users, and comes amid a broader reckoning across the globe over those effects.

Meta has said penalties could be as high as $US1.4 trillion ($1.9 trillion), close to the California-based company's market value.

Attorneys-general have yet to specify penalties but said at a hearing last week the amount could be closer to $US200 billion ($282 billion) — equivalent to about three years of after-tax profit for Meta.

Meta ordered to pay $538m in US trial The verdict marks the first time a jury has ruled on such claims against Meta, as the company faces a wave of lawsuits over how its platforms affect young people's mental health.

California, Colorado, Kentucky and New Jersey also want Meta to implement age restrictions, eliminate the infinite scroll that encourages users to keep looking at new posts, and make other changes to its platforms.

In a statement before the trial, a Meta spokesperson said the states' claims were unsubstantiated and the company stood by its record of creating strong protections for teenagers.

"The [attorneys-general] offer no proof anyone in their states was misled, claim benign features like having an additional Instagram account somehow harmed their residents, and attempt to penalise Meta for industry-wide challenges like age verification," the spokesperson said.

"Rather than sticking to the facts or the law, the states have instead decided to chase an outlandish payout."

Multi-state investigation

The lawsuit began in 2023 and stemmed from a multi-state investigation into Instagram and Facebook's impact on young users.

That followed testimony by whistleblower Frances Haugen, who told a US Senate committee in 2021 that Meta knew its products could harm young users and knew how to make them safer, but chose not to make changes in favour of pursuing higher profits.

Social media ban spreads More and more countries are following Australia's lead and introducing social media bans for children, but US policies are piecemeal and vary from state to state.

The states are expected to present a trove of internal documents and research from Meta, and testimony from former Meta employees and experts.

Meta and other social media companies including Snap Inc, TikTok parent ByteDance and YouTube parent Alphabet face thousands of lawsuits by states, municipalities, school districts and individuals over whether their products harm young users.

In March, a Los Angeles jury ordered Meta and Google to pay $US6 million ($8.5 million) to a 20-year-old woman who said she became addicted to Instagram and YouTube media as a child.

Earlier this month, a New Mexico judge ordered Meta to pay $US567 million ($800 million) into a mental health fund for teenagers after that state's attorney-general said the company's platforms were a public nuisance.

Reuters

World.title: Jailed former Pakistan PM Imran Khan moved to hospital over health concerns
World.content:
Pakistan's Supreme Court has ordered former prime minister Imran Khan be moved to hospital from jail, meeting a longstanding demand of his party and family, who had raised concerns about his health.

Cricketer-turned-politician Khan, 73, has been in jail in the garrison town of Rawalpindi since August 2023, convicted in a string of cases that he says were politically driven following his ouster in 2022.

His sons repeatedly expressed concern regarding his deteriorating health last year, with his lawyers saying he had lost significant vision in his right eye while in prison.

"Mindful of the fundamental right, we are issuing this order to ensure health and safety of the prisoner," said Justice Shahid Waheed, head of the three-judge bench that heard the petition.

The court directed that Khan be moved to Shifa International Hospital in the capital Islamabad within 48 hours and remain there until September 16, Khan's spokesperson Naeem Haider Panjutha said on X.

A judge ordered supporters of the former Pakistani prime minister stay away from the hospital he has been taken to. (Reuters: Fayaz Aziz)

It also ordered the creation of a medical panel for his treatment, including a cardiologist, general medicine specialist, eye specialist and Khan's personal physician.

Khan's Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) party welcomed the order, saying it should be implemented "immediately, fully, and without delay".

"We wish it had happened sooner so his eye and general health would not have deteriorated this much," PTI spokesperson Zulfikar Bukhari said.

The party also appealed to its members and Khan's supporters not to gather outside the hospital, in accordance with the court's order.

No reaction from government

There was no reaction from the government to the court order and the information and interior ministries did not respond to Reuters' requests for comment.

Khan's younger son, Kasim, said his health was "all that mattered".

"We hope the government adheres to the court orders … allows calls and issues our visas to Pakistan simply so we can come and see him," he said in a statement shared with Reuters.

Thousands of Imran Khan's supporters have taken to the streets in recent years to protest his imprisonment. (AP: Irtisham Ahmed )

Kasim and his older brother Sulaiman — raised in Britain after Khan's divorce from their mother, British socialite and filmmaker Jemima Goldsmith — have not seen their father since 2022 in the absence of a visa.

Since he lost power in a no-confidence vote, Khan has faced multiple cases, including over state gifts and an accusation of an unlawful marriage. Some convictions have been suspended or overturned, with appeals pending. He denies wrongdoing.

Khan's initial arrest in May 2023 sparked protests that saw hundreds of people attacking state buildings and rampaging through military installations.

His supporters have similarly taken to the streets on several occasions in the years since to demand his release.

Cricket greats from around the world, including from across the border in rival India, demanded better treatment for Khan in February, expressing "deep concern" about his prison conditions.

The government had denied allegations of mistreatment.

PTI won power in 2018 and retains a large support base across key provinces but was stripped of its election symbol ahead of the 2024 vote.

Its candidates, who were forced to contest as independents, won the most seats in the election but fell short of the majority needed to form a government.

Reuters

World.title: Government to crack down on super switching schemes
World.content:
Unlicensed telemarketers that cold call and make unsolicited approaches to convince people to switch their super will be banned under long-awaited reforms.

Assistant Treasurer Daniel Mulino will appear at the National Press Club today and announce a suite of reforms to better protect Australians from falling victim to operators that rob them of their retirement savings.

The reforms follow the collapse of the Shield and First Guardian funds that saw 12,000 people lose more than $1 billion in retirement savings, and which exposed deep flaws in the regulation of Australia's almost $4.5 trillion retirement savings pool.

Currently, people might go on Facebook and click an ad that looks innocent like "Find Your Lost Super" or "Check Your Super", but then gives permission for a telemarketer, also known as a "lead generator", to contact them and suggest they connect with a financial adviser to switch their super.

Mr Mulino said, under the changes, in order to be able to advertise, these lead generators would need to be licensed.

Daniel Mulino will present superannuation reforms at National Press Club. (ABC News: Stuart Carnegie)

It stops short of the outright ban on advertising that some consumer groups have been calling for.

The assistant treasurer said there would be "exceptions" to protect advocacy, educational and employment communications.

Deep flaws in Australia's $4.3 trillion system exposed The collapses of the First Guardian and Shield schemes have exposed deep flaws in the regulation of Australia's $4.3 trillion superannuation sector.

"These reforms are designed to disrupt some of the most damaging business models operating in the system today," Mr Mulino said.

"They target the point at which consumers are first exposed to harm and reduce the ability of bad actors to gain access to consumers in the first place."

Mr Mulino said he also wanted to "strengthen the anti‑hawking regime to enhance consent requirements, limit the existing financial advice exemption to existing client relationships and strengthen penalties for breaches".

That would require licensees "to take reasonable steps to ensure lead generation activities comply with relevant regulatory and legal requirements".

Super telemarketers lure investors in

Michael Johnson is one of thousands of investors who lost his retirement savings, along with his wife, Caroline, when First Guardian collapsed in April 2025.

They each had separate superannuation accounts with retail funds, but in October 2020 moved about $500,000 of their super from APRA-regulated funds into one joint self-managed superannuation fund (SMSF).

Michael Johnson and his wife lost $500,000 of their retirement savings. (ABC News: John Gunn)

Mr Johnson said he decided to switch his super after seeing an  on Facebook, and then being contacted by a lead generator, who eventually put them onto financial advisers at United Global Capital (UGC).

ASIC to review super 'lead generators' ASIC is investigating whether lead generators are complying with their legal obligations when suggesting people switch their retirement savings into less-regulated investment schemes.

"It was just like other ads you see for changing your health insurance or your car insurance, and it said, 'Do a health check on your super,'" he said.

That call from the telemarketer quickly led to him connecting with financial advisory firm UGC, which convinced him and his wife to move all their super and invest it wholly in the First Guardian Master Fund.

UGC entered liquidation in August 2024 and ASIC cancelled the advisory firm's Australian Financial Services Licence (AFSL) in July 2024.

The primary adviser from UGC involved was contacted for comment but did not respond.

Mr Johnson said the financial advisers "were very convincing", but that had the government regulated lead generators before he and his wife switched their super, "we wouldn't have gone in at all".

Telemarketers, also known as lead generators, contact people after the click on social media ads and give their contact details. (iStock: Tero Vesalainen)

"Part of how this worked was a remarkably large number of people signing up at the same time," Mr Johnson said.

" The operators … constructed a scheme that was based on getting lots of people in quickly, grabbing that money and then going home and then disappearing with it. "

Mr Johnson said at the time he invested, First Guardian was described to the couple as a "diversified" investment vehicle.

He didn't realise anything was wrong until it was too late.

Proposed levy could cost self-managed super funds The assistant treasurer is looking to revamp funding for the Compensation Scheme of Last Resort, saying that large super funds, as well as people with self-managed super funds (SMSFs), could be asked to chip in.

"It was devastating," Mr Johnson told ABC News.

"We're approaching retirement. Caroline was looking at reducing her work hours. We wanted to be able to retire and keep our current lifestyle."

Mr Johnson said the couple now did not know how they could financially manage.

"It looks like we will be needing to have a government pension and the whole point of having compulsory superannuation is that you don't need [to do] that," he said.

" It's impacted our mental health. That impacts our physical health. It's made life seem much harder. "

Call for social media companies to take down 'harmful' ads

Super Consumers CEO Xavier O'Halloran supports the ban on unlicensed cold calling, but wants to see obligations on social media platforms to take down harmful ads.

ASIC warns on online trading platforms A review of nine online trading companies finds several are encouraging Australians to jump on "complex" deals, putting them at risk of major losses.

He said that through lead generators, consumers' details then got sold on to a financial advisor "where you're put into really a train towards selling you financial advice, often quite expensive, over $10,000 in some cases, and getting you to switch into certain products".

"We still want to see greater protections and obligations on the social media platforms to ensure that these ads are taken down if there are still harmful ones being put up," he said.

Xavier O'Halloran wants to see obligations on social media platforms to take down harmful ads. (ABC News: John Gunn)

"We don't want to see claims made that can't be substantiated. We don't want to see people's details collected then on-sold to someone else without their knowledge.

"We don't want … what is meant to be a basic health check on their superannuation, then suddenly sold into very expensive financial advice that sees them switched into really inappropriate products and have their entire retirement savings wiped out."

CSLR changes could impact payouts

Today, Mr Mulino is also expected to announce changes to the Compensation Scheme of Last Resort (CSLR), which covers victims of financial misconduct who have not been compensated for their losses — up to $150,000.

He is expected to widen the number of sectors that pay the levy to fund the scheme, which will include big super funds.

The "but for" test, which considers whether a claimant would have been in a better financial position had they received appropriate advice and earned interest, is expected to be removed.

The "but for" test has faced criticism from some in the advice industry for using a definition that's too broad, but consumer groups argue that removing it punishes victims of misconduct.

Stronger obligations on super platforms to check the investments they offer and act when things go wrong are also anticipated, along with stronger powers for ASIC to make platforms pay if they fail to protect their customers.

Mr Mulino is expected to unveil financial advice reforms to make financial advice more affordable and accessible to a broader range of consumers.

Michael Johnson said he and his wife Caroline had made a complaint to the Australian Financial Complaints Authority (AFCA) to recover their super lost in the First Guardian collapse, but that the body was still investigating their claim.

If their claim fails, or if AFCA cannot recover the money from UGC, the couple will have to rely on the CSLR.

The CSLR will treat the couple's claims as one claim, and the $150,000 cap falls well short of their total losses.

Mr Johnson said if their retirement money had stayed in performing superannuation funds, he estimated that, together, they would have accumulated about $1.3 million in retirement savings by now.

ABC Business Daily The podcast that helps you unpack the latest business and finance news.

Super Consumers' Mr O'Halloran was concerned removing the "but for" test would punish consumers and urged victims of the First Guardian and Shield collapses to claim before it is removed.

"For a typical person that was invested in Shield and First Guardian — if they don't get their complaint in by July 1 of 2027 — they could miss out on any investment earnings that they would have otherwise received in compensation," he said.

Mr O'Halloran said people who lost their life savings in the Shield and First Guardian collapses lost an average of $100,000, and Super Consumers' modelling found the government's proposed change could cost them another $26,500 in lost investment earnings.

" We don't think victims should be punished for the collapse of these financial schemes. They should be properly compensated and we [the government and regulators] should go after the actual criminals. "

Mary Delahunty, chief executive of the Association of Superannuation Funds of Australia (ASFA), welcomed the changes to ensure unlicensed lead generation operators were banned.

But she was unhappy that super funds were being tapped to pay for growing claims under the CSLR.

"It is not okay that superannuation funds have been co-opted into paying for a scheme that the majority of their members cannot claim from," Ms Delahunty said.

"What that amounts to is like a tax on every Australian to pay for a scheme that, yes, needs to exist, but not in its unsustainable form.

"So this is an ongoing point that we need to work with the government on."

Mary Delahunty says super funds should not be tapped to pay for the CSLR levy. (ABC News: Paul Pandoulis)

Sarah Abood, CEO of the Financial Advice Association Australia (FAAA), welcomed the minister's expected change to broaden the scope of financial advice consumers can access.

"Financial advice has never been more important, but too many Australians simply cannot afford it," she said.

"Australians need a financial advice system that is affordable, accessible and trustworthy."

World.title: Cannabis use and psychosis are linked, but study finds age matters
World.content:
Cannabis-users who develop psychosis in their 30s experience symptoms more than six years earlier on average than people with the condition who don't use the drug, according to new research.

These figures are in sharp contrast to younger age groups, with cannabis-users in their early 20s who develop psychosis doing so on average about 1.6 years earlier than non-users, and no evidence of earlier onset in those under 20.

The study's senior author, University of New South Wales (UNSW) researcher Matthew Large, said the association between using cannabis and the early onset of psychosis had already been suggested by previous studies.

But in this new large-scale analysis, published today in Biological Psychiatry, Dr Large said researchers were able to examine an "enormous amount of data" and use "fine grain analysis" to look at age sub-groups for the first time.

People experiencing psychosis often feel disconnected from reality, and struggle to distinguish between what's real and what isn't.

The older the age group was, Dr Large explained, the larger gap there was between cannabis-users and non-users in regards to the age when symptoms of psychosis first appeared.

"It was widely assumed that the earlier age of onset of [psychosis] mostly affected young people. This study shows, contrary to that expectation, that it mostly affects people in their late 20s and over 30s," he said.

" That is a finding that has not been demonstrated in any other study, [it] hasn't even been suggested. "

About 2.5 million people in Australia use cannabis every year. (Getty Images: Creative Images Lab)

The study's lead author, UNSW academic and medical student Carly Stevens, said this suggested the harm could be "cumulative".

"There seems to be this predominant idea of the adolescent brain being very vulnerable, which is true," she said.

Using cannabis at a young age can disrupt neurodevelopmental processes in the adolescent brain, influencing how the brain develops, affecting the memory, attention and growth.

"But also this prevailing myth that if you wait until your brain develops, and then you engage in these kind of behaviours, that you'll be OK," she said.

"But our findings likely show that in terms of the onset of psychosis, it's not younger people that are at risk, but actually older people."

Earlier in life, Ms Stevens said genetic vulnerability and neurodevelopmental factors could play a greater role as there was very little time for cannabis to have an influence.

But, she said, ongoing cannabis use could lower the threshold for when symptoms of psychosis first appeared later in life.

More data, same results

Dr Large, who is a clinician and works directly with patients, said about 3 per cent of people will experience psychosis at some point in their lives and 1 per cent will develop schizophrenia, which is a lifelong condition.

A similar large-scale analysis led by Dr Large and published in 2011 probed 83 studies and found the mean age of psychosis onset for cannabis-users was 2.7 years younger than non-users.

This new analysis, which looked at 149 international studies involving more than 71,000 people, suggested the age of psychosis onset for cannabis-users was 2.5 years earlier, on average.

Dr Large said the similarities between the two suggested the overall conclusion was robust.

Cannabis and psychosis: how strong is the risk? Psychotic disorders are severe mental health condition and there's consistent evidence showing a link between heavy or repeated cannabis use and an experience of psychosis for the first time.

Jack Wilson, a research fellow at The University of Sydney's Matilda Centre who did not contribute to the study, said it added to "the growing body of evidence" that cannabis use was associated with a greater risk of developing psychosis.

"It's certainly providing new evidence on the likelihood of developing psychotic disorders in different age groups, according to whether someone is using cannabis or not," he said.

"And that is quite concerning, given the relative ease at which we can now access increasingly potent cannabis products in Australia."

Dr Wilson said higher consumption of tetrahydrocannabinol or THC was "associated with the greater risk of harm".

One of the study's limitations was that it didn't probe the type of cannabis products that were being used, Dr Wilson said, and extra information about potency would be useful to know.

With about 2.5 million Australians using cannabis a year, Dr Large said he was also concerned that cannabis potency was increasing over time, describing some as "amazingly potent".

Young people still at risk

Despite the study's stark findings about older Australians who use cannabis, Ms Stevens said it was important to note that younger people were certainly not immune to harm.

"Everyone, no matter the age, is at risk of some kind of adverse event from using cannabis," she said.

Dr Wilson agreed, adding that the accelerated onset of psychosis was just one measure of harm.

"There is no safe time to use cannabis, but the most dangerous or the most harmful time to use cannabis is at a younger age, particularly before the age of 25, when we're still seeing neurodevelopment," he said.

While more research was needed, Dr Wilson said changes in the developing brain could contribute to the development of psychiatric disorders, such as schizophrenia.

If possible, Dr Wilson urged people to avoid more potent products, which had the potential to cause not just psychosis, but greater overall harm.

"Delay the onset of use. We know that harm is greatest in those that are using cannabis at a younger age," he said.

"We also know that you know that smoking cannabis is associated with cardiovascular risk, so if people can avoid smoking and perhaps avoid mixing with tobacco."

Prompting calls for more health warnings

Researchers are now calling for greater public health messaging about the use of cannabis regardless of whether it is used recreationally or as a legal medicinal product.

They would also like to see stronger regulations regarding the sale of medicinal cannabis in Australia.

Medicinal cannabis is regulated in Australia and must be prescribed by a registered healthcare professional.

Guidelines suggest it cannot be used as a first-line treatment.

Ms Stevens said as a scientist, she wasn't able to provide an in-depth answer about best-practice legislation, but said the way medicinal cannabis was being marketed and sold in Australia was "quite inappropriate".

ABC Health in your Instagram feed Follow @abchealth on Instagram, where we're busting myths and sharing practical, smart health advice.

She said some providers selling medicinal cannabis claimed to operate under Therapeutic Goods Administration (TGA) guidelines, claiming to be "fully TGA-approved".

But most medicinal cannabis products are classed as unapproved therapeutic goods, which means they have not been assessed for safety, quality or efficacy.

Dr Large was more scathing in his assessment.

"I personally think that the medicationalisation of [cannabis] has quashed the discussions about the toxicity of cannabis," he said.

" It's that part of public policy that I think will quite likely prove to be one of the biggest public health bungles in Australian history. "

World.title: Ten killed after Russian missiles hit shops in Ukrainian village
World.content:
A Russian missile attack has killed 10 people in a village in Ukraine's north-eastern Kharkiv region, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said, as he vowed that Kyiv would respond.

There was no immediate comment from Russia on the attack, which also injured at least 18 people, according to the regional governor.

"This morning, the Russians launched a brutal attack on a busy intersection in Pechenihy, Kharkiv region — a location with a post office and stores, surrounded only by residential buildings," Mr Zelenskyy said on X.

"We will definitely respond to this Russian strike," he added.

Reuters video from Pechenihy showed several covered bodies lying on the ground, burnt-out cars and damaged buildings.

Russia has intensified its air attacks on Ukraine over the summer, trying to exploit its smaller neighbour's critical shortage of interceptors capable of downing ballistic missiles.

Cafe and post office among shops hit

The United Nations said last week that civilian casualties from the war in Ukraine had risen by nearly a third month-on-month in July.

The UN Human Rights Monitoring Mission in Ukraine said on X it was gathering information about the attack in Pechenihy and its impact on civilians.

Ukraine is upping strikes on Russia in a bid to pressure Vladimir Putin to the negotiating table. (Reuters: Alexander Kazakov)

Ukraine has also increased its attacks on Russia, targeting oil facilities and logistics infrastructure to try to undermine Moscow's ability to wage war.

On Tuesday, Moscow's mayor said Ukraine had launched 620 drones at the Russian capital and surrounding areas, in one of Kyiv's biggest air assaults on the region.

Both Russia and Ukraine deny deliberately targeting civilians in their attacks.

The strike on Pechenihy village injured at least 18 people and damaged 10 private buildings, a cafe, a post office, five stores and 15 cars, the governor of the surrounding region, Oleh Syniehubov, said on the Telegram messaging app.

According to preliminary information, Russia used two small Banderol cruise missiles in the attack, the office of Ukraine's Prosecutor General said.

A local official told public broadcaster Suspilne that the strikes had hit the central part of the village, where the cafe, post office and shops are located.

Drone hits near nuclear power plant

In a separate strike on Tuesday, local time, the International Atomic Energy Agency said a drone exploded at a bus stop used by staff of Ukraine's Zaporizhzhia nuclear power plant, killing one and injuring several others.

The IAEA, the United Nations' nuclear power watchdog, in a statement on X also said the plant's director described the incident as "the worst event the plant has faced".

Russia currently controls the Zaporizhzhia Nuclear Power Plant in southern Ukraine. (Reuters: Alina Smutko)

The agency, citing the plant's director, said the explosion at around 6am caused 16 casualties among staff and subcontractors, including one death and three serious injuries.

Russian forces seized the station, Europe's largest with six reactors, in the first weeks of their February 2022 invasion of Ukraine, and each side has since regularly accused the other of actions compromising nuclear safety.

UK backs Ukraine after Russian threat

Meanwhile, the UK's new prime minister is vowing the country will continue to support Ukraine "100 per cent", after Russia's embassy in the country threatened consequences over Kyiv's use of British-made drones.

British newspaper The Sunday Times earlier this week reported that two UK companies made drones used by Ukraine to hit Russia.

Following the report, the Russian embassy in the UK said in a statement that "London's actions will inevitably carry consequences".

That led British Prime Minister Andy Burnham to publicly commit that the UK "stands 100 per cent behind Ukraine".

A spokesperson for the UK's defence ministry has also weighed in, saying that: "Britain stands shoulder to shoulder with Ukraine, and we are committed to providing the equipment Ukraine needs to defend itself against Putin's illegal invasion."

Reuters/AP

World.title: US calls Israeli strike on Syrian air base 'unnecessary escalation'
World.content:
The United States has condemned Israeli air strikes on a Syrian air base, labelling it an "unnecessary escalation" and insisting the new Syrian government is not the threat the Netanyahu government argues it is.

Syrian state television has reported eight Israeli airstrikes hit the Abu al-Duhur base in the north west of the country, 70 kilometres from the Turkish border.

The Ekhbariya outlet reported the base's runway and storage facilities were hit, citing a Syrian military source.

The Israeli military has yet to comment.

In a statement, the Syrian foreign ministry condemned the attacks and described them as an "unjustified act of aggression, a flagrant violation of Syria's sovereignty and territorial integrity, and a dangerous escalation that threatens security and stability in the region".

It said the "Syrian state has exercised restraint and worked to consolidate stability and avoid escalation" with Israel, despite coming under repeated attacks since early December 2024, when the former Assad regime was toppled.

That sentiment was shared by the US Ambassador to Turkiye and special envoy for Syria and Iraq, Tom Barrack.

"The Al-Sharra government has neither adopted a predatory posture nor maintained proxy forces," he posted on X.

"It has, in fact, repeatedly indicated a preference for de-escalation with Israel.

"The United States has in the past, and will continue in the future, to host discussions to encourage diplomatic cadence over kinetic frustration for both nations."

Mr Barrack said countries should "prioritise logical discourse over further military incidents".

Israel at odds with US over closer Syria ties

Benjamin Netanyahu's Israeli administration has expressed its deep concerns about the new Syrian government, led by former rebel leader Ahmed Al-Sharaa.

Mr Al-Sharaa, a former Al Qaeda commander, swept to power in December 2024 as his forces ended the five-decade long Assad family dictatorship.

While publicly stating he wants to unify the civil war-ravaged country, Israel has cited Mr Al-Sharaa's history and ties to extreme Islamist ideology to justify its own "security" measures against Syria.

Syrian President Ahmed Al-Sharaa said he aims to unify the war torn country. (Reuters: Yves Herman)

This has included deploying Israeli forces into south-western Syria, beyond the border of the occupied Golan Heights, and launching strikes on some towns and cities in the area.

On Tuesday, Israel’s Foreign Ministry pointed to video which had spread on social media over the weekend purportedly showing Syrian soldiers chanting violent and threatening remarks against Jews.

Why did Israel reject Gaza plan? Israel's rejection of Donald Trump's Gaza peace plan is not a surprise. Here's why and how politics plays into it ahead of an Israeli election.

It has put Israel at odds with the United States, and particularly Donald Trump's White House, which has fostered deeper ties with the new Syrian government.

That has included lifting crippling economic sanctions against Syria, and even inviting the president to the White House — a move which would have been unthinkable just a few years ago, when Mr Al-Sharaa was subject of a US bounty.

In recent months, the Syrian government has tried to rebuild the country's air force — something Israel has seen as another threat to its own security.

With Reuters

World.title: ‘Meta needed kids’: Tech giant on trial over social media addiction
World.content:
WorldNorth AmericaSocial media ‘Meta needed kids’: Tech giant on trial over social media addiction Diana Novak Jones August 19, 2026 — 3:20am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A coalition of US states suing Meta Platforms over claims Facebook and Instagram were designed in ways that harmed young users’ mental health began making its case in a California federal court, in a trial that could reshape some of the most popular apps on the planet. Megan O’Neill, a deputy California attorney general, told the eight-person jury in Oakland, California on Tuesday (US time) that Meta’s business model was to “hook the users, hold them for as long as they can, harvest their data, and then hide the truth from the public”. “It worked especially well for kids,” she added. The Ronald V. Dellums Federal Building and US Courthouse in Oakland, California. Bloomberg O’Neill told the jury the case was not about taking away Instagram, or social media.



“This case is not about whether social media has some benefits for some people. It does,” she said. California, Colorado, Kentucky and New Jersey are leading a bipartisan group of 29 states suing Meta. Related Article Social media Meta and Google found liable in landmark social media addiction trial Jurors are expected to issue an advisory verdict, but US District Judge Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers will determine Meta’s liability. If she finds Meta liable, Rogers could impose civil penalties and order changes to Facebook and Instagram. The trial will address claims by the four lead states that Meta designed Facebook and Instagram to addict young children and teenagers, resulting in such harms as anxiety, depression and even suicide, and misled consumers about the platforms’ safety.



“Meta needed kids, and it needed to reassure the people who cared about those kids that the kids are safe,” O’Neill said. Jurors will also hear claims by all 29 states that Meta violated federal law by improperly collecting and using personal data of children while they used its platforms. California Attorney General Rob Bonta arrives at the courthouse on Tuesday. AP Photo/Noah Berger Lawyers for Meta are expected to tell the jury that the company has made a huge effort to keep kids safe online. Meta has said it did not make misleading statements about safety, and the states failed to show their residents were harmed. Meta co-founder and chief executive Mark Zuckerberg and Instagram chief Adam Mosseri are expected to testify. The trial is scheduled to last six weeks.



Experts have said the trial is the biggest legal test yet of social media’s effects on young users, and comes amid a broader reckoning across the globe over those effects. Meta has said penalties could be as high as $US1.4 trillion ($1.97 trillion), close to the Menlo Park, California-based company’s market value. Attorneys general have yet to specify penalties but said at a hearing last week the amount could be closer to $US200 billion – equivalent to about three years of after-tax profit for Meta. California, Colorado, Kentucky and New Jersey also want Meta to implement age restrictions, eliminate the infinite scroll that encourages users to keep looking at new posts, and make other changes to its platforms. Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg, pictured in February, is expected to give evidence. Bloomberg



In a statement before the trial, a Meta spokesperson said the states’ claims are unsubstantiated and the company stands by its record of creating strong protections for teenagers. “The AGs offer no proof anyone in their states was misled, claim benign features like having an additional Instagram account somehow harmed their residents, and attempt to penalise Meta for industry-wide challenges like age verification,” the spokesperson said. “Rather than sticking to the facts or the law, the states have instead decided to chase an outlandish payout.” The lawsuit began in 2023 and stemmed from a multistate investigation into Instagram and Facebook’s impact on young users. Related Article Online gambling Facebook is advertising illegal gambling, and the watchdog is powerless to stop it That followed testimony by whistleblower Frances Haugen, who told a U.S. Senate committee in 2021 that Meta knew its products could harm young users and knew how to make them safer, but chose not to make changes in favour of pursuing higher profits.



The states are expected to present a trove of internal documents and research from Meta, and testimony from former Meta employees and experts. Meta and other social media companies including Snap Inc, TikTok parent ByteDance and YouTube parent Alphabet face thousands of lawsuits by states, municipalities, school districts and individuals over whether their products harm young users. In March, a Los Angeles jury ordered Meta and Google to pay $US6 million to a 20-year-old woman who said she became addicted to Instagram and YouTube media as a child. Earlier this month, a New Mexico judge ordered Meta to pay $US567 million into a mental health fund for teenagers after that state’s attorney general said the company’s platforms were a public nuisance. Reuters

World.title: Give renters a break: Two-year leases plan to protect from ‘gouging’ landlords
World.content:
PoliticsFederalProperty prices Give renters a break: Two-year leases plan to protect from ‘gouging’ landlords Shane Wright August 19, 2026 — 12:01am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Renters would be offered at least two-year tenancy deals and billions of taxpayers’ dollars spent on new public housing under a plan from the ACTU as it pushes for the Albanese government to build on its negative gearing and capital gains tax reforms. As new figures suggest tentative signs of a slowdown in runaway rents, particularly in regional parts of the country, the union movement believes the nation’s millions of tenants need greater protection from “rent-gouging professional landlords”. The peak body for Australian unions wants to fight for two-year leases. Peter Rae The ACTU backed the May budget overhaul of property taxes that, combined with higher interest rates and low affordability, have contributed to a slowdown in property prices. Economists are tipping falls of up to 14.5 per cent in Sydney over the next 18 months before a recovery in 2028. The drop in prices comes off a peak that has left almost every capital city among the most expensive in the world. Rents have also soared by more than 20 per cent since the end of the freeze on increases introduced during the early stages of the COVID pandemic.



ACTU president Michele O’Neil said there had to be better protections for renters, especially over the length of their tenancy agreements. Loading She said the minimum tenancy should be increased from one year to two, with renters able to negotiate a shorter period if they wanted. “Our housing system should reflect the reality that millions of working people are renters. Workers deserve not only secure jobs, but also secure housing. Unions want to see renters with stronger rights, better protections against evictions and more secure leases,” O’Neil said. “Doubling the default rental standard from one to two years would still allow renters to choose shorter leases, but it would give workers more certainty and stability to plan their lives.”



On top of longer leases, unions want a national regulator of all rentals and tighter eviction procedures. Related Article Property prices Air is coming out of the housing bubble. Is now the time for first home buyers? Apart from increasing tenure security for renters, the ACTU on Wednesday will also launch a campaign for a major increase in government spending on public housing. It wants the state and federal governments to set a target of 10 per cent of all new housing stock to be public housing, with the aim of 6 per cent of all homes being public. There are about 300,000 public homes in Australia at present. Ten per cent of all new homes would add 20,000 properties to the stock of public homes each year.



“Under the Hawke government, one in 10 new homes built were public housing, but today that’s closer to 1 in 50. If we’re serious about fixing the housing crisis, we must increase public housing stock to free up homes in the private rental market and make renting more affordable for everyone,” O’Neil said. On Tuesday, shadow treasurer Tim Wilson accused the Albanese government of deliberately pushing up rents to contribute to a lift in inflation to help its budget bottom line. “We have an active inflation agenda from the Albanese government, and it’s leading to higher rents by design in their budget so they can get more tax revenue,” he said. Treasurer Jim Chalmers rejected suggestions the budget changes would lead to a surge in rents, noting Treasury had estimated the budget tax changes would add less than $2 a week to the median rent. “The best way to assess the impact of these policies is over the next couple of years, not over the first couple of months,” Chalmers told the Nine Network.



Related Article Trade unions ACTU leaders to go by year’s end after COVID, CFMEU saga “Building more homes is our primary objective, but also reforming the tax system to make it fairer for first home buyers. Those two things over time will pay off.” Research released on Wednesday by Cotality suggests some of the heat is coming out of the rental market. In an update on regional property markets, it found that vacancy rates – although still well below long-term average – had increased over the past three months with a slight slowdown in rents. Sydney’s vacancy rate has climbed to 2.1 per cent, after hovering close to 1 per cent for much of the past two years. In Melbourne, it has increased to 1.5 per cent after being around 1.1 per cent for much of 2024.



The tightest rental markets are in regional Australia, including 0.8 per cent in the NSW coastal centre of Forster-Tuncurry and 0.9 per cent in the Victorian regional city of Warrnambool. Cotality’s head of research Gerard Burg said regional property markets were starting to soften like the capital cities. “Rental growth has moderated alongside broader housing market conditions, but vacancy rates remain relatively tight across many regional centres,” he said. World.title: Brace yourselves: The finals won’t be a consideration for Sydney
World.content:
Analysis SportAFLAFL off-field behaviour Brace yourselves: The finals won’t be a consideration for Sydney Jake Niall August 18, 2026 — 11:40pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

If the Swans followed the standard script for AFL clubs on the eve of finals, they would be pushing for a two-match ban for the players who have caused such embarrassment to the club, the game and themselves. Expediency and the necessity of retaining their gun players would win out if they followed the old template. Swans coach Dean Cox and CEO Matthew Pavlich. Artwork: Michael Howard Quietly, a modern version of “boys will be boys” would be whispered. The club would fight and lawyer up to ensure that their foolish four or five would play, at worst, in the second week of the finals (not counting the wildcard games). But this is not the vibe that is wafting out of Swans headquarters or the AFL. At no stage have excuses or justifications been peddled in an attempt to minimise the damage.



At no stage have they, or the AFL, disparaged or blamed the women who were in the hotel room when the alleged incident occurred that has led to a police investigation for a possible sexual assault. Loading The Swans are incensed by the gigantic own goal that the players have scored in the social realm – the ramifications of which go well beyond the finals and the impact on that campaign. We should take them at their word. Their statement to media, issued before the Tuesday-night board meeting that would shape their proposed sanctions, did not read well for those hoping for a convenient two-game ban.



One could be misreading it, but the language used suggested that the players would be missing for more than two games. This column does not promote gambling, but if the betting agencies placed the line at two matches, I’d be taking overs. The Swans said they believe the players “are in serious breach of expected club behaviour and standards”, foreshadowing “firm action”. They made plain that sanctions would be entirely separate from the police investigation, which is ongoing, with no arrests or charges laid. Two matches, including a dead rubber in round 24, would hardly cut it as “firm action”. The statement added: “The club also acknowledges that these serious allegations impact others and their wellbeing must be paramount.



“The Sydney Swans condemn all forms of abuse and disrespectful behaviour towards women. Any conduct that causes offence or harm to others is unacceptable and falls well short of our expectations. All women deserve to be respected and feel safe.” Photo: Matt Golding The statement’s concern for Sydney’s AFLW players and program was telling. “We also want to acknowledge that the care and welfare of our AFLW athletes and staff is of the utmost importance to us as a club,” the club continued. “They have been and will continue to be offered the support they require and we acknowledge the impact these allegations have on our female athletes, staff members and the wider community.” The words deployed by the Swans don’t sound at all like a club that is focusing only on finals.



The impression is that they are thinking beyond the immediate horizon of September, that they understand the deeper ramifications to their club’s reputation, to its cultural foundations, and that respect for women isn’t simply a convenient platitude for government funding and sponsors. Related Article Investigation

AFL off-field behaviour A handful of Swans players wanted to keep partying. The fallout has rocked the AFL Further, their statement accorded with that of AFL chief executive Andrew Dillon, who has been dealing with both Sydney CEO Matthew Pavlich and the club’s experienced chairman Andrew Pridham since the police investigation detonated on Monday. Tom Harley, the AFL senior executive who handles integrity and immediate past CEO of the Swans, is doubtless another important figure in the dialogue between his former club and the league. In scandals past, the AFL has hovered over clubs, prodding and pushing them to swallow suspensions.



This time, the Swans and the AFL seem as aligned as a club and league can be in a stressful scenario for both parties. Keep up to date with the best AFL coverage in the country.

World.title: Melbourne dealt massive finals blow as star forward’s ban upheld
World.content:
Updated SportAFLAFL 2026 Melbourne dealt massive finals blow as star forward’s ban upheld Jon Pierik Updated August 18, 2026 — 10:09pm ,first published 11:36am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Three-game AFL striking ban upheld for van Rooyen AAP Melbourne have suffered a major pre-finals blow, potentially losing key forward Jacob van Rooyen for the rest of the AFL season through suspension. The Demons failed in their bid to have van Rooyen’s three-game ban for striking overturned or reduced. Joe Richards remonstrates with Jacob van Rooyen after the incident with Aliir Aliir. AFL Photos



It means he will miss the fifth-placed Demons’ final home-and-away game on Saturday against the Western Bulldogs, and that Melbourne will need to win two finals for him to play again this season. Van Rooyen is having a career-best season, kicking 42 goals in 22 games. The Demons forward was charged with striking after he concussed Port Adelaide defender Aliir Aliir in a marking contest on Saturday night at Adelaide Oval. It was graded as severe impact, careless conduct and high impact. Loading After the 90-minute hearing, where van Rooyen testified that he was trying to mark the ball when he collected Aliir, the tribunal jury deliberated for nearly an hour before upholding the charge.



Melbourne had argued van Rooyen’s attempt to mark the ball was not careless, but the tribunal rejected their case. Tribunal chair Jeff Gleeson KC also turned down a bid from the Demons to have a biomechanist give evidence for van Rooyen. “The swing of Van Rooyen’s left arm constituted the act of a strike. It was a forceful blow. It was not simply a trailing or leading arm that Aliir collided with,” Gleeson said in the verdict, adding the panel found it was careless. “Van Rooyen was initially intending to mark the ball, but we find that shortly before impact, he ceased to intend to mark the ball. We say this despite van Rooyen’s evidence to the contrary. “Even if it was van Rooyen’s sole objective at all times to contest the mark, we find that he did so in a way that failed to take reasonable care to avoid acts which could be reasonably foreseen to result in a reportable offence.



“Van Rooyen had time to move his right arm in response to seeing Aliir and he could have done so to some extent or sufficient extent with his left arm.” Why Viney’s September dreams hang in the balance Jon Pierik Melbourne vice captain Jack Viney faces a race against time to return for the finals despite a successful comeback through the VFL. Viney had 19 disposals, including a goal and a game-high 10 clearances, for Casey in the VFL in his comeback from Achilles tendon and back issues.



Demons vice captain Jack Viney hasn’t played a senior game this season, but is now pushing for a return. Getty Images He had not played a game at all this season, one in which the Demons have rebounded from a horror 2025 to be in the frame for a top-four finish heading into Saturday’s clash against the Western Bulldogs – the final game of the home-and-away campaign. Adding to the Demons’ dilemma is that Casey’s VFL campaign has ended, finishing the year 18th on the ladder. While coach Steven King was delighted with Viney’s return, he said on Tuesday there was much to consider when it came to the midfielder’s possible senior return. “There’s a lot of factors that go into it. Obviously, the team balance. We’ve won six of our last seven, but, I mean, when you have Jack Viney available, it’s only a good thing,” King said.



Related Article Analysis

AFL 2026 From football glory to police investigation: The 12 hours that changed everything for the Swans “So, I want to make sure I do the right thing by the team, the club, but more so Jack as well. We want to make sure when he comes in, he’s really ready. Is that this week? We’ll wait and see.” The Demons’ midfield has been purring, so Viney would have to squeeze into a line-up that included dynamic playmaker Kysaiah Pickett, the newly contracted Tom Sparrow, Caleb Windsor and Joel Fitzgerald. The Demons are hoping to be involved in a VFL scratch match this weekend to give several of their fringe players another chance to push for finals selection. “I think we have to acknowledge that VFL and AFL are different sports. The intensity … you can’t replicate an AFL game,” King said.



“In saying that, we are in a position with five on the bench. We’d be able to manage players coming back in like we do. I think every team would have probably one player that spends a little less game time, so that’s definitely an option. “For me, we just have to look at our mix and our balance, and there’s more to it than just one player comes in. It’s the ripple effect, how it affects your team and your squad, and also your opponents who are playing that week.” Viney is contracted until the end of 2028. King said he was delighted that Sparrow had inked a five-year deal, and said skipper Max Gawn, almost certain to be named an All-Australian for the ninth time, should also be bestowed the captaincy.

World.title: The VISA hits the fan
World.content:
When the well-travelled Graham Cochrane (C8) made mention of an unwelcome S.H.I.T. stamp, Granny must confess to feeling rather unworldly, but then Steve Castieau of Bexley came along to explain: “In the 1970s, long-haired overland travellers entering Malaysia from Thailand often had their visas marked S.H.I.T (Suspected Hippy In Transit) accompanied by a stern warning to travel directly to Singapore. Entry into Singapore usually required the inevitable haircut.”

“In 1977, when I was considered to be a long-haired uni layabout by some, I travelled to New Zealand for a camping trip,” says Tim Ingall of Scottsdale Arizona, USA. “It took an hour to clear customs as a suspicious, older customs agent went through my gear looking for drugs including probing each aluminium tent pole. On returning to Australia I anticipated similar customs duty interrogation. Instead, I got a ‘G’day’, followed by a short question: ‘Are you bringing any drugs into the country?’ I answered no and was immediately sent on my way. Good thing I wasn’t doing anything nefarious – or at least that’s my story, and I’m sticking to it 49 years later!”

Stephen Tait of Bellevue Hill noticed that Janice Creenaune (C8) was visiting Dirranbandi, Queensland and is hoping “can she report on the welfare of the Norton Brothers and in particular Les Norton? All are robust and handy employees at the Dirranbandi Pub.”

More on the dreaded restaurant dress code (C8), from Elsa Cant of Merewether. “We presented at a posh hotel in London with my husband wearing a very nice (and expensive) leather jacket. This was deemed not respectable and was taken from him and replaced with a too-small, faded, red suit jacket. Thus, he was now suitably dressed for entry to the restaurant for afternoon tea.” As a waiter?

“Pleasing it is to report the first magpie sighting in full swooping mood on a cyclist here in Mudgee,” says Simon Staines. “Is this the earliest reporting of our beloved and most accomplished songbird in action I ask?”

World.title: ‘Meta needed kids’: Tech giant on trial over social media addiction
World.content:
WorldNorth AmericaSocial media ‘Meta needed kids’: Tech giant on trial over social media addiction Diana Novak Jones August 19, 2026 — 3:20am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A coalition of US states suing Meta Platforms over claims Facebook and Instagram were designed in ways that harmed young users’ mental health began making its case in a California federal court, in a trial that could reshape some of the most popular apps on the planet. Megan O’Neill, a deputy California attorney general, told the eight-person jury in Oakland, California on Tuesday (US time) that Meta’s business model was to “hook the users, hold them for as long as they can, harvest their data, and then hide the truth from the public”. “It worked especially well for kids,” she added. The Ronald V. Dellums Federal Building and US Courthouse in Oakland, California. Bloomberg O’Neill told the jury the case was not about taking away Instagram, or social media.



“This case is not about whether social media has some benefits for some people. It does,” she said. California, Colorado, Kentucky and New Jersey are leading a bipartisan group of 29 states suing Meta. Related Article Social media Meta and Google found liable in landmark social media addiction trial Jurors are expected to issue an advisory verdict, but US District Judge Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers will determine Meta’s liability. If she finds Meta liable, Rogers could impose civil penalties and order changes to Facebook and Instagram. The trial will address claims by the four lead states that Meta designed Facebook and Instagram to addict young children and teenagers, resulting in such harms as anxiety, depression and even suicide, and misled consumers about the platforms’ safety.



“Meta needed kids, and it needed to reassure the people who cared about those kids that the kids are safe,” O’Neill said. Jurors will also hear claims by all 29 states that Meta violated federal law by improperly collecting and using personal data of children while they used its platforms. California Attorney General Rob Bonta arrives at the courthouse on Tuesday. AP Photo/Noah Berger Lawyers for Meta are expected to tell the jury that the company has made a huge effort to keep kids safe online. Meta has said it did not make misleading statements about safety, and the states failed to show their residents were harmed. Meta co-founder and chief executive Mark Zuckerberg and Instagram chief Adam Mosseri are expected to testify. The trial is scheduled to last six weeks.



Experts have said the trial is the biggest legal test yet of social media’s effects on young users, and comes amid a broader reckoning across the globe over those effects. Meta has said penalties could be as high as $US1.4 trillion ($1.97 trillion), close to the Menlo Park, California-based company’s market value. Attorneys general have yet to specify penalties but said at a hearing last week the amount could be closer to $US200 billion – equivalent to about three years of after-tax profit for Meta. California, Colorado, Kentucky and New Jersey also want Meta to implement age restrictions, eliminate the infinite scroll that encourages users to keep looking at new posts, and make other changes to its platforms. Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg, pictured in February, is expected to give evidence. Bloomberg



In a statement before the trial, a Meta spokesperson said the states’ claims are unsubstantiated and the company stands by its record of creating strong protections for teenagers. “The AGs offer no proof anyone in their states was misled, claim benign features like having an additional Instagram account somehow harmed their residents, and attempt to penalise Meta for industry-wide challenges like age verification,” the spokesperson said. “Rather than sticking to the facts or the law, the states have instead decided to chase an outlandish payout.” The lawsuit began in 2023 and stemmed from a multistate investigation into Instagram and Facebook’s impact on young users. Related Article Online gambling Facebook is advertising illegal gambling, and the watchdog is powerless to stop it That followed testimony by whistleblower Frances Haugen, who told a U.S. Senate committee in 2021 that Meta knew its products could harm young users and knew how to make them safer, but chose not to make changes in favour of pursuing higher profits.



The states are expected to present a trove of internal documents and research from Meta, and testimony from former Meta employees and experts. Meta and other social media companies including Snap Inc, TikTok parent ByteDance and YouTube parent Alphabet face thousands of lawsuits by states, municipalities, school districts and individuals over whether their products harm young users. In March, a Los Angeles jury ordered Meta and Google to pay $US6 million to a 20-year-old woman who said she became addicted to Instagram and YouTube media as a child. Earlier this month, a New Mexico judge ordered Meta to pay $US567 million into a mental health fund for teenagers after that state’s attorney general said the company’s platforms were a public nuisance. Reuters

World.title: Give renters a break: Two-year leases plan to protect from ‘gouging’ landlords
World.content:
PoliticsFederalProperty prices Give renters a break: Two-year leases plan to protect from ‘gouging’ landlords Shane Wright August 19, 2026 — 12:01am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Renters would be offered at least two-year tenancy deals and billions of taxpayers’ dollars spent on new public housing under a plan from the ACTU as it pushes for the Albanese government to build on its negative gearing and capital gains tax reforms. As new figures suggest tentative signs of a slowdown in runaway rents, particularly in regional parts of the country, the union movement believes the nation’s millions of tenants need greater protection from “rent-gouging professional landlords”. The peak body for Australian unions wants to fight for two-year leases. Peter Rae The ACTU backed the May budget overhaul of property taxes that, combined with higher interest rates and low affordability, have contributed to a slowdown in property prices. Economists are tipping falls of up to 14.5 per cent in Sydney over the next 18 months before a recovery in 2028. The drop in prices comes off a peak that has left almost every capital city among the most expensive in the world. Rents have also soared by more than 20 per cent since the end of the freeze on increases introduced during the early stages of the COVID pandemic.



ACTU president Michele O’Neil said there had to be better protections for renters, especially over the length of their tenancy agreements. Loading She said the minimum tenancy should be increased from one year to two, with renters able to negotiate a shorter period if they wanted. “Our housing system should reflect the reality that millions of working people are renters. Workers deserve not only secure jobs, but also secure housing. Unions want to see renters with stronger rights, better protections against evictions and more secure leases,” O’Neil said. “Doubling the default rental standard from one to two years would still allow renters to choose shorter leases, but it would give workers more certainty and stability to plan their lives.”



On top of longer leases, unions want a national regulator of all rentals and tighter eviction procedures. Related Article Property prices Air is coming out of the housing bubble. Is now the time for first home buyers? Apart from increasing tenure security for renters, the ACTU on Wednesday will also launch a campaign for a major increase in government spending on public housing. It wants the state and federal governments to set a target of 10 per cent of all new housing stock to be public housing, with the aim of 6 per cent of all homes being public. There are about 300,000 public homes in Australia at present. Ten per cent of all new homes would add 20,000 properties to the stock of public homes each year.



“Under the Hawke government, one in 10 new homes built were public housing, but today that’s closer to 1 in 50. If we’re serious about fixing the housing crisis, we must increase public housing stock to free up homes in the private rental market and make renting more affordable for everyone,” O’Neil said. On Tuesday, shadow treasurer Tim Wilson accused the Albanese government of deliberately pushing up rents to contribute to a lift in inflation to help its budget bottom line. “We have an active inflation agenda from the Albanese government, and it’s leading to higher rents by design in their budget so they can get more tax revenue,” he said. Treasurer Jim Chalmers rejected suggestions the budget changes would lead to a surge in rents, noting Treasury had estimated the budget tax changes would add less than $2 a week to the median rent. “The best way to assess the impact of these policies is over the next couple of years, not over the first couple of months,” Chalmers told the Nine Network.



Related Article Trade unions ACTU leaders to go by year’s end after COVID, CFMEU saga “Building more homes is our primary objective, but also reforming the tax system to make it fairer for first home buyers. Those two things over time will pay off.” Research released on Wednesday by Cotality suggests some of the heat is coming out of the rental market. In an update on regional property markets, it found that vacancy rates – although still well below long-term average – had increased over the past three months with a slight slowdown in rents. Sydney’s vacancy rate has climbed to 2.1 per cent, after hovering close to 1 per cent for much of the past two years. In Melbourne, it has increased to 1.5 per cent after being around 1.1 per cent for much of 2024.



The tightest rental markets are in regional Australia, including 0.8 per cent in the NSW coastal centre of Forster-Tuncurry and 0.9 per cent in the Victorian regional city of Warrnambool. Cotality’s head of research Gerard Burg said regional property markets were starting to soften like the capital cities. “Rental growth has moderated alongside broader housing market conditions, but vacancy rates remain relatively tight across many regional centres,” he said. Getty Images He had not played a game at all this season, one in which the Demons have rebounded from a horror 2025 to be in the frame for a top-four finish heading into Saturday’s clash against the Western Bulldogs – the final game of the home-and-away campaign. Adding to the Demons’ dilemma is that Casey’s VFL campaign has ended, finishing the year 18th on the ladder. While coach Steven King was delighted with Viney’s return, he said on Tuesday there was much to consider when it came to the midfielder’s possible senior return. “There’s a lot of factors that go into it. Obviously, the team balance. We’ve won six of our last seven, but, I mean, when you have Jack Viney available, it’s only a good thing,” King said.



Related Article Analysis

AFL 2026 From football glory to police investigation: The 12 hours that changed everything for the Swans “So, I want to make sure I do the right thing by the team, the club, but more so Jack as well. We want to make sure when he comes in, he’s really ready. Is that this week? We’ll wait and see.” The Demons’ midfield has been purring, so Viney would have to squeeze into a line-up that included dynamic playmaker Kysaiah Pickett, the newly contracted Tom Sparrow, Caleb Windsor and Joel Fitzgerald. The Demons are hoping to be involved in a VFL scratch match this weekend to give several of their fringe players another chance to push for finals selection. “I think we have to acknowledge that VFL and AFL are different sports. The intensity … you can’t replicate an AFL game,” King said.



“In saying that, we are in a position with five on the bench. We’d be able to manage players coming back in like we do. I think every team would have probably one player that spends a little less game time, so that’s definitely an option. “For me, we just have to look at our mix and our balance, and there’s more to it than just one player comes in. It’s the ripple effect, how it affects your team and your squad, and also your opponents who are playing that week.” Viney is contracted until the end of 2028. King said he was delighted that Sparrow had inked a five-year deal, and said skipper Max Gawn, almost certain to be named an All-Australian for the ninth time, should also be bestowed the captaincy.
