World.title: The VISA hits the fan
World.content:
When the well-travelled Graham Cochrane (C8) made mention of an unwelcome S.H.I.T. stamp, Granny must confess to feeling rather unworldly, but then Steve Castieau of Bexley came along to explain: “In the 1970s, long-haired overland travellers entering Malaysia from Thailand often had their visas marked S.H.I.T (Suspected Hippy In Transit) accompanied by a stern warning to travel directly to Singapore. Entry into Singapore usually required the inevitable haircut.”

“In 1977, when I was considered to be a long-haired uni layabout by some, I travelled to New Zealand for a camping trip,” says Tim Ingall of Scottsdale Arizona, USA. “It took an hour to clear customs as a suspicious, older customs agent went through my gear looking for drugs including probing each aluminium tent pole. On returning to Australia I anticipated similar customs duty interrogation. Instead, I got a ‘G’day’, followed by a short question: ‘Are you bringing any drugs into the country?’ I answered no and was immediately sent on my way. Good thing I wasn’t doing anything nefarious – or at least that’s my story, and I’m sticking to it 49 years later!”

Stephen Tait of Bellevue Hill noticed that Janice Creenaune (C8) was visiting Dirranbandi, Queensland and is hoping “can she report on the welfare of the Norton Brothers and in particular Les Norton? All are robust and handy employees at the Dirranbandi Pub.”

More on the dreaded restaurant dress code (C8), from Elsa Cant of Merewether. “We presented at a posh hotel in London with my husband wearing a very nice (and expensive) leather jacket. This was deemed not respectable and was taken from him and replaced with a too-small, faded, red suit jacket. Thus, he was now suitably dressed for entry to the restaurant for afternoon tea.” As a waiter?

“Pleasing it is to report the first magpie sighting in full swooping mood on a cyclist here in Mudgee,” says Simon Staines. “Is this the earliest reporting of our beloved and most accomplished songbird in action I ask?”

World.title: Documents reveal Health NZ hiring crackdown
World.content:
Health NZ leaders told the Health Minister tight controls on hiring staff were crucial to delivering its budget and that recruitment of any frontline worker was only possible with the sign-off of senior executives.

In a briefing to Simeon Brown last March, then-Health Commissioner Professor Lester Levy and interim chief executive Dr Dale Bramley said strict recruitment rules had been in place throughout 2024/25, and frontline hiring decisions required the sign-off of the regional deputy chief executive.

"This has been coupled with regular close monitoring of recruitment pipelines and the establishment of the HR oversight group," Levy and Bramley wrote. "The expectation is for these controls to remain in place throughout 2025/26."

The documents were released under the Official Information Act to the Public Service Association (PSA), which says Health NZ intentionally delayed recruitment, leaving patients and health workers suffering as a result.

In the same briefing, Levy and Bramley said there would be control over clinical safety, so there were no compromises made to services.

PSA national secretary Fleur Fitzsimons said that was "pure fantasy", saying that roles weren't advertised or filled for months at a time, leading to chemotherapy services being shut down and stroke patients not getting the regular care they deserved.

"These documents expose that the health minister was aware that our health system was not filling hospital vacancies as part of a deliberate savings plan and that patient care has suffered as a result. It's scandalous."

The health minister's office said he told the agency late last year to eliminate bureaucracy in hiring. Health NZ says it no longer uses regional panels for budgeted staff.

'Complex, bureacratic approval system'

An internal document in June 2024 from then-chief executive Margie Apa showed four regional recruitment forums were set up to approve all hospital and specialist service roles.

An organisation-wide hiring freeze was put in place for all non-frontline roles. This applied to all hospital roles that did not deal directly with patients and all public health jobs that did not deal directly with the community.

The forums included regional directors, medical, nursing, allied health, rural decision-makers, as well as finance and P&C enablers, and were required to regularly sign off hiring decisions.

Fitzsimons said the approval systems were complex and beauratic, taking the hiring decisions away from the hospital and service level.

"The approval would take months. In one case, we had a payroll officer, needing to be approved by the chief executive, before the vacancy was advertised.

"Health New Zealand set up a complex, bureacratic approval system in order to slow down recruitment and save money, and the minister knew about it."

PSA national secretary Fleur Fitzsimons said recruitment delays severely affeced patients. Supplied

The entire Health NZ northern region, which has more than 20,000 employees, was limited to hiring 40 full time roles a fortnight, claimed a union report, called Vacant by Design.

The report quoted workers who described the process as involving "multiple layers of internal and national approvals".

The union said the requirement for regional deputy directors to also sign off frontline staff meant local decisions were made too far away from where the vacancy was.

"The decision about whether to replace an emergency department administrator in Gisborne was made in Hamilton, while the decision about whether to approve a mental health worker in Kaitaia was made in Auckland," the report said.

Six months to fill three neonatal nurse roles

Fitzsimons said the slow recruitment process led to "harrowing examples" of health services being understaffed, with some vacancies not even advertised for months.

"It took six months to replace three neo-natal intensive care nurses in Wellington, a Northland radiologist vacancy sat unapproved for 12 weeks, we saw a regional sonologist vacancy - 28 weeks before it was approved to be filled.

"We are seeing a deliberate strategy, driven by Simeon Brown, where hospital vacancies are not being filled, because they want to save money."

Other examples included an intensive care nurse in the Wellington region not approved after 19 weeks, an emergency department nurse in the southern region not approved for five weeks, a midwife in Counties Manukau not approved after seven weeks and a cardiology service administration clerk not approved 10 weeks later, the report said.

A survey of 1800 PSA members said 76 percent of their team waited more than a month for approval to fill vacancies, and 85 per cent said unfilled roles drove colleagues to stress and burnout.

Fitzsimons said the delayed hiring process led to stroke patients suffering.

Stroke patients should be seen every day, but were commonly only being seen three times a week, impacting their ability to make meaningful progress, the union report said.

In July, Brown announced hospitals could recruit and deploy staff without central sign-off, reducing response times when demand rises, but Fitzsimons said the policy was far from over.

"There is an approval system for new roles in our hospitals that means vacancies are taking too long to be filled and it needs to stop."

Health minister, Health NZ respond

A spokesperson from Brown's office referred to a Letter of Expectations Brown sent to Health NZ in November 2025.

"The minister's position was clear that Health New Zealand 'must continue to remove unnecessary bureaucracy to ensure clinical appointments are delivered in a timely manner, particularly in geographic locations or services experiencing workforce shortages that are directly impacting on patient care'."

A Health NZ spokesperson said it had now changed its hiring processes and the four regional recruitment panels no longer existed.

Current recruitment processes for budgeted roles were now 'two-up', involving the hiring manager's manager, he said.

Management, admin or other roles that weren't budgeted for may need regional review from a forum or committee.

Health NZ introduced a devolved operating model earlier in 2026 to ensure decisions were clinically led and met local need, the spokesperson said.

"While planning and strategy remain a national function, healthcare decisions - including recruitment - are being made closer to care."

The spokesperson said Health NZ did not accept the suggestion recruitment decisions were deliberately leaving services understaffed or that they compromised patient safety.

"Recruitment decisions are made based on service need, workforce availability and patient safety."

World.title: Plans unveiled for major Okains Bay Museum redevelopment
World.content:
Banks Peninsula's Okains Bay Museum has unveiled design plans for a major redevelopment the board says is essential to protect its precious displays.

The museum opened in 1976 and houses a nationally significant collection of more than 20,000 Māori and colonial artefacts.

The board asked MAP Architects to develop concept plans for a new whare taonga and upgrades to the wider museum complex, which have been published on the museum's website.

The board asked for a new whare taonga and upgrades to the wider museum complex. Supplied

The board was now working with Christchurch City Council on district planning requirements and consenting processes, before embarking on community consultation.

A fundraising campaign was expected to follow, although the cost of the proposed redevelopment was yet to be determined.

Outgoing board chair Helen Brown said the current building was not fit for purpose.

"The current building in which the taonga Māori are housed has sub-optimal conditions. It is a building which fails on multiple levels. It doesn't meet best practice standards and it is prone to temperature and humidity fluctuations," she said.

Brown said a feasibility study was carried out in 2020 and the board decided to develop the concept plans last year.

The current museum building RNZ / Nate McKinnon

The long house would emulate a wharenui or farm shed and the courtyard of heritage buildings relocated from around Banks Peninsula would remain, she said.

"That character that many people know and love will remain," Brown said.

"The building that is called the colonial hall will remain but will be refitted and has a facade added to the front. There is a link building that connects that building to a new long house.

"This is all aspiration of course and concept level at this stage."

Brown said the museum board also wanted to incorporate public amenities, including community and education spaces and after-hours toilets.

The board said the plans visualised "enhanced collection storage, refreshed exhibition spaces and flexible new areas that can be used by local community and school groups and pre-booked tours for years to come".

The museum marked 50 years of hosting the South Island's biggest and longest-running Waitangi Day commemorations on 6 February.

The museum and annual event were the brainchild of the museum's founder Murray Thacker, whose passion for preservation formed the foundation of the collection, from waka to wagons, taonga puoro (traditional Māori instruments), kitchenalia, a blacksmiths forge and hei tiki.

The museum began as Thacker's private collection, as the great grandson of some of the earliest Pākehā settlers in Okains Bay.

World.title: Growing homelessness linked to tighter emergency housing rules, community leader says
World.content:
A community housing leader says there is a direct link between growing homelessness and the government's decision to tighten emergency housing eligibility.

However, the responsible minister says the stricter criteria were implemented along with increased support for those in need.

In recent times, about a third of emergency housing applications to the Ministry of Social Development are being declined each month, according to the agency's latest figures released to RNZ under the Official Information Act.

Before August 2024 - when stricter rules about getting into and staying in emergency housing came into force - decline rates were in the single digits.

That came a few months after the Government set a target to reduce the number of households in emergency housing by 75 percent, saying motels weren't appropriate for families, especially children.

Community Housing Aotearoa chief executive Paul Gilberd said the data spoke for itself.

"One can clearly see the policy direction, the moment in time when the policy direction to the MSD staff was changed, the steep and significant decline in emergency and special needs grants, and the corresponding increase in rough sleeping around the country."

Gilberd said while there was "a lot of debate" about exact homelessness figures, data gathered by community groups showed "it's at the highest level it has ever been".

He said there was consensus that children should not grow up in emergency housing motels, but reducing their use had left some without alternatives.

"It's a lose-lose scenario for everybody who is involved. It's not great for the staff at MSD. It's definitely not a great outcome for our rough sleeping and homeless communities, and it's not a really good outcome for taxpayers because where they're ending up is in the emergency departments and in Corrections."

Paul Gilberd RNZ / Edward O'Driscoll

MSD figures from June show the most common reason for declining emergency housing applications is "the need can be met another way" (about 27 percent of 729 rejections), followed by "you have caused or contributed to your immediate need" (about 19 percent).

The latter category was among several new criteria introduced in mid-2024, intended to "tighten the gateway" to emergency housing.

MSD officials told ministers at the time the changes risked increasing homelessness, particularly for children, Māori, and people with complex needs.

However, unlike other criteria, Ministers decided MSD staff should have discretion about whether to apply the "caused or contributed to your immediate need" test to an applicant.

"An option considered was making 'contribution to immediate EH [emergency housing] need' a compulsory consideration. However, this determination is a subjective assessment, and can risk excluding people with an immediate EH need, exacerbating support needs and therefore creating a long-term fiscal cost," the report read.

Gilberd described determining whether someone contributed to their homelessness as "deeply problematic", as it required frontline staff to make subjective decisions with imperfect information.

"We know that our rough sleepers and homeless, who have typically had quite a bad experience of life and of agencies, are deeply reluctant to be fully clear and transparent and share all of their personal information when they walk into an MSD office and meet a case manager."

In March, an Auditor-General report into housing needs recommended MSD staff guidance be updated to ensure assessments about "contributing" to one's need for emergency housing be clarified - something the agency had since done.

Gilberd said the core issue was the lack of affordable housing due to underinvestment by successive governments.

He said he was agnostic about who would supply that housing - be it Kāinga Ora, community housing providers, iwi, or churches.

"Until we decide as a society and give the signals to our politicians that it's going to be safe for them to get re-elected by having a policy which invests significant additional new money into this supply, this problem is not going to go away."

Associate Housing Minister Tama Potaka RNZ / Samuel Rillstone

Potaka: Emergency housing changes appropriate

Associate Housing Minister Tama Potaka said the government's tightening of emergency housing grants in 2024 "restored emergency housing to its purpose as a last resort".

He said the changes came alongside increased support for people with housing needs, as well as more public and transitional housing.

"Our Government has always wanted, and continues to want, people to have a safe and secure roof over their heads, not to be left living in a hotel room," Potaka said in a statement.

"Emergency housing was never intended to become a long-term home for thousands of families. We set a target to reduce the number of households in emergency housing by 75 percent by 2030, and achieved it five years early."

He said about 70 percent of those not granted emergency housing were offered alternative support, such as transitional housing, help to remain in their current home, or assistance securing a private rental.

As for the remaining 30 percent, Potaka told the Herald in June: "Some of those people may well be in housing now, some of them may not be."

Potaka says the government "restored emergency housing to its purpose as a last resort". RNZ / Rayssa Almeida

Meanwhile, MSD told RNZ last month people were under no obligation to tell the agency where they were living.

Karen Hocking, MSD's enablement group general manager, said emergency housing applications were most often declined when applicants had other options available, such as staying with family or friends.

"We may also decline someone's application if their situation is a result of their own actions, or actions of people they are responsible for, and they were reasonably able to predict and prevent it," she said in a statement.

"For example, people are generally expected to organise somewhere new to live before they leave their existing accommodation. If someone chooses to give up their tenancy without a good reason and without making other arrangements, they are likely to have unreasonably caused or contributed to their immediate need."

Hocking said people leaving their homes due to family violence would not be considered to have contributed to their need.

World.title: Christopher Luxon, Chris Bishop press fondness for Hutt Valley in show of party unity
World.content:
Prime Minister Christopher Luxon and Chris Bishop - one of his ministers accused of trying to topple him last week - were all smiles at a public meeting in the latter's electorate on Tuesday night.

Leadership squabbles escaped any mention, with just one veiled reference to politics being a "tough sport" in opening remarks.

"It's a rough game, we know that."

About 250 people turned out on a wet Tuesday evening the Fraser Park Events centre in Avalon, Lower Hutt where a brick near the entrance is adorned with the words: Chris Bishop MP for Hutt South.

It's a title the Attorney-General, Minister for Housing, Infrastructure and Transport will want to retain in this year's election - particularly given a combination of low polling and high numbers of electorate wins could turf him out of Parliament altogether.

Bishop praised his party leader, calling Luxon the man in charge of National's plan who was doing "an outstanding job".

National leader Christopher Luxon at the podium at the Fraser Park Events centre in Avalon in Lower Hutt. Sanele Chadwick/RNZ

He said Luxon had got into politics and Parliament for the right reasons, "dedicating his life to public service to try and make a difference for all of us".

Luxon in turn gave acknowledgement to "the great Chris Bishop".

"If you cut him, he bleeds the Hutt. That's what he believes. He eats, breathes, sleeps it. He's talking about it every Tuesday in our caucus room.

"So, mate, thank you for your public service because you've been a dedicated public servant and representative for this region for some time," he said, later praising his third-ranked MP for his work on the Resource Management Act reforms.

Luxon's speech warned the world was at an "inflection point" of mass change.

"Turn on the six o'clock news and you see things like countries that used to be friends with each other actually squabbling and fighting ... wars in Ukraine in the middle of Europe, but also in the Middle East, we see trade wars flaring between countries that we thought were friends and alliance partners.

"We had a similar experience after World War I; after World War II; certainly after the fall of the [Berlin] Wall in 1989; and I put it to you, since 2024. The world has been changing in terms of how it deals with each other and works together or doesn't."

He pitched himself as an "outside politician" who had "watched them for years just boil the ocean, lots of bumper stickers, lots of promises", when people wanted "delivery".

Several questions Luxon answered effectively but with the usual party lines, or asking audience members to "watch this space" for future party policy announcements.

Chris Bishop and Christopher Luxon arrive at the meeting. Sanele Chadwick/RNZ

FENZ in firing line

Perhaps the most heated was about why - given Labour sorted union negotiations out with firefighters after the first ever nationwide strike - National hasn't done the same after 54; and why a community centre burned down about 550 metres from the previous fire station that got shut down.

Bishop said Fire and Emergency (FENZ) was a "shocker" at managing their assets.

"I have been pushing them and the Minister of Internal Affairs, Brooke van Velden, very hard to say what is the plan around the Hutt City fire station, and I just get crickets in response because you've got an incompetent governence and management there ... I'm furious about it."

Luxon said the "bottom line is, they have money. They have enough money".

About 250 people turned out on a wet night to listen to the two politicians. Sanele Chadwick/RNZ

The prime minister refused to commit to not lowering funding for kindergartens, but again said there would be more policy to come.

When asked how National could help conservative voices in local government to oppose Labour and Green councillors, Luxon said "if only 30 percent of you bother to vote in a local body election, you kind of get what you deserve".

In response to questions about removing climate change from curriculums, he said the first thing was getting kids to school, then teaching them to read and do maths, before giving them the foundations to engage in science and climate change.

Bishop kept the last question for himself to ask Luxon about his connection to the Hutt Valley, saying few people may know he began at Unilever in Petone.

"I am a Crusaders supporter, you know that and we've just lost the whole room now," Luxon quipped.

"That business, they had a big factory down the bottom end of Jackson Street and so I came here as the brand manager for Sunlight dishwash liquid, Jif cream cleanser and Handy Andy ... as a 22, 24 year old.

"It was an amazing place to live, and I'm really grateful for the start that business gave me, but also the city gave me that then led me to live overseas for 16 years doing some other things with that same business."

He finished with a joke about hearing a "massive rumble" after moving to Sydney and getting under his desk thinking it was an earthquake, but the Australian marketing director said it was just a truck from the factory.

Luxon and Bishop then spoke to those in attendance and took selfies for about another half hour.

Those in attendance had mixed views of the discussion, with some National supporters saying it was great, and good to hear from the prime minister with full context rather than in soundbites.

Several undecided voters who spoke to RNZ remained unconvinced, saying their votes had not been swayed at all.

World.title: US siblings become NZ refugees as more than 20 Americans claim asylum
World.content:
Government figures show more than 20 Americans have applied for asylum in New Zealand since 2020 - and at least one family was accepted.

Failed US appeals have centred on fears of gun crime, the environment and political climate.

Two American asylum claims of a brother and sister were successfully appealed, because of concerns their dual US/Jordan nationalities would lead them into harm.

Their Jordanian mother had been granted refugee status in New Zealand after she was repeatedly assaulted by her husband while living here, and treated as a servant by his extended family while living in Jordan.

She did not have US citizenship and so could not move there with her 11-year-old son and seven-year-old daughter. She and her husband had divorced, and she had custody of their children.

The tribunal ruled that if the pair were not given refugee status in New Zealand, the US was likely to send them back to Jordan where 'the children would be at risk of breach of their right to be free from cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment'.

"In Jordan, they fear being placed in the custody of their father's family and being mistreated by members of their paternal and maternal families," the tribunal said in its decision about the children.

"In the United States, they fear living as unaccompanied minors in institutional or foster care, and that they will be refouled [sent back] to live with family in Jordan."

Their mother had moved to New Zealand with her husband in 2011 when he was a student, saying she suffered intimate partner violence from the start, and was later abused by their families in Jordan.

"The mother was treated by her extended family like a servant and punished for not getting along with her husband. The [children] were treated cruelly by the mother's father, and the father's brothers hit and yelled at the son for any minor wrongdoing. The father's mother also encouraged the son to hit his sister and to censure her."

The family returned to New Zealand, but the violence continued, they were divorced and police were called after she was hospitalised by her injuries. The Family Court made an order barring the father from taking the children overseas.

"The mother also fears that her former husband's family will apply to the United States authorities for the children to return with them to Jordan and they will be exposed to ongoing violence in Jordan at their hands," said the children's 2023 appeal at the immigration and protection tribunal. "She fears, in particular, for her daughter, who will be raised in a climate of violence, and be conditioned to be a subordinate female accustomed to accepting violence."

Among unsuccessful US asylum bids was a woman who wanted protection from Covid-19, gun crime and her own government.

"The tribunal drew the appellant's attention to country information which indicated that while the USA is: politically and socially divided, has high rates of gun ownership, is suffering a rise in belligerent violent anti-government rhetoric, particularly on the far-right such that many people subjectively fear the country is heading towards civil war, the chance that a violent 'civil war' would erupt was remote and speculative."

Despite a significant number of Covid deaths and hospitalisations, "contrary to common parlance, there is in fact no recognised human right to be healthy", and the USA was complying with its obligations.

In another case, an American man claimed he risked persecution for expressing his anti-government views.

"The risk of the appellant being seriously harmed in the United States through environmental degradation, nuclear and toxic waste accidents, or gun-related violence is entirely remote and speculative and well below the 'real chance' threshold," it concluded.

"While the tribunal has no doubt the appellant is sincere in his beliefs and in his desire to live in New Zealand, a country to which he evidently feels a greater affinity than his native United States, the Refugee Convention is not designed to provide a pathway to residence for persons who feel morally and politically disassociated from the direction of their country."

A bisexual Jewish man afraid of returning to the US after president Donald Trump was first elected, also had his appeal dismissed on similar grounds.

A 1995 tribunal finding underpins some of the reasoning: "in the case of an advanced western democracy which generally respects the rule of law, such as the United States, there is a presumption of state protection" of citizens' rights, it said.

A 2008 appeal remarks that the-then Refugee Status Authority "has been unable to establish that there has ever been a successful claim for refugee status made in respect of a person being returned to [the US], either as a national or as a former habitual resident."

Many of the asylum claims cited fear of gun violence, while one man appeared to be fleeing justice.

"He claims that he will be immediately arrested on return to the United States, on the basis of a false criminal record and, owing to his profile, may be held in detention. He claims that he will not be able to seek redress from the US courts and may be repeatedly incarcerated and frustrated by [an unnamed State] District Attorney." He claimed risks to his personal security and freedom from threats made to him as a whistle-blower.

A 68-year-old woman believed Islamist terrorists had killed her relatives in America and had tried to kill her too, but was believed to be suffering from mental health problems. A 42-year-old man said he feared the extent of police violence, as he had been arrested for illegal camping during an Occupy protest, and had been criticised for his political beliefs.

Non-genuine asylum-seekers

Tribunal cases feature some asylum seekers who it decides genuinely fear for their safety or rights but do not meet criteria for asylum - for example, if the chance of someone being persecuted is remote.

However, migrants have also been accused of using the system to instead pursue the work rights that come with an asylum claim.

"While there are genuine claims, there are many claims - the vast majority of claims - that are not meritorious," immigration minister Erica Stanford said in March, as she pointed to high rejection rates of asylum claims.

"And in some instances, people lodge an asylum claim in the final days of another visa, not because they face persecution in their home country, but simply because they want to remain in New Zealand on that visa that everybody wants, the open work visa."

The Age in Australia reported on Sunday that 230 UK citizens in the last year had claimed asylum, with suggestions they were part of a trend of visa overstayers finding a legal loophole to stay and work in Australia.

In New Zealand, refugee claims are still dominated by people from India (683 last year) and China (336). Alongside the US, unusual source countries in the past three years include six Irish asylum seekers and five Japanese.

World.title: Espionage at scale - why businesses must beware
World.content:
This year's security threat report names China to an unusual extent, leaving questions around whether the wording might provoke our 'complicated, but important' trading partner

The NZSIS 2026 Security Threat Environment report didn't hold back about intensified threats to the country's security, naming interference in our elections, efforts to get hold of critical assets - including high-tech secrets from the space sector - targeting of our diaspora community groups, and homegrown threats and violence from extremists.

Something else it named? China.

In the past, such reports have tread a delicate diplomatic balance, wary of offending our notoriously tetchy trade partner and avoiding singling out any one particular nation - but the language this year has been specific.

The report talked about the People's Republic of China being the only country detected conducting espionage at scale, China trying to get information about our critical assets that "cannot be described as benign" and a Communist Party research institution called the Purple Mountain Observatory, saying it had tried to use trickery to get satellites up and running here.

The spy agency was able to disrupt its attempts, but the threat report said it wasn't the first attempt and was unlikely to be the last.

"This was a really clear and solid example of one of the ways that China is trying to get critical infrastructure in our part of the world," says Anna Fifield, former Washington Post Beijing bureau chief, and now The Detail's Saturday host specialising in geo-politics.

"We hear a lot about how they are trying to repress diaspora communities, trying to influence certain elections, but this was a really concrete example of how a Chinese state-affiliated research institute had used a cover story to try to trick a New Zealand company into letting them install ground-based space infrastructure, which is basically radar or antenna like that from which they can monitor activity in space."

On The Detail today, Fifield talks about the balancing act in such reports, when it comes to warning Kiwi companies about what's going on, without offending the Chinese, our largest trading partner.

"The SIS was really clear in its report to say 'this should not deter companies'. Most of the business we do with China is all above board, but they are warning companies, New Zealand institutions, universities that work in these sensitive areas where dual-use technology could be in place just to be aware, on the alert about this and to go to them with any questions.

"I think it's about raising awareness that not all Chinese activity is benign. If China comes back and tries to do this in another way, hopefully they will catch it earlier."

Fifield also says these SIS threat reports have become progressively more direct in calling out China by name.

"It's quite a sharp change for New Zealand and it's one that Australia hasn't made. Their equivalent security threat assessment report does not name China by name, it just refers to 'foreign actors' or 'third countries'... so it is unusual, but I think it really re-inforces the threat that our officials, our spooks, see from China... trying to take advantage of our naivety, take advantage of our good trading relationship with them and use that for their purposes.

"In this kind of situation, they will deny all knowledge usually, and say that China abides by rules and international law, and expects everybody else to do the same. I certainly don't think that China is going to 'fess up to this, but it will be on their radar - no pun intended!"

So far, in reaction to the SIS report, the Chinese embassy in Wellington has said it "fabricates and hypes", and has even suggested that the report itself may well be the result of foreign interference - "part of a new round of attacks, smears and vilification of China orchestrated by certain international forces".

The Chinese state-affiliated Global Times reported that China "firmly rejected and condemned" the report, "stressing that the report is rife with Cold War thinking and contains unfounded accusations against China".

The article also quotes an academic who called it 'compensatory hawkishness', with the goal of proving New Zealand's reliability as a Five Eyes ally.

Fifield says we may not have heard the last of this from Beijing and there's always the chance of trade retaliation.

"China makes a habit of using its economic power as political leverage, there is always the chance they will do that with New Zealand. Luckily we have avoided that so far, but our exporters are certainly alert to the risk of that and trying to factor that in.

"I think even our big exporters know that there are going to be times when Chinese behaviour is so egregious that our government will have to issue statements in this way about it.

"If it wants to be angry about something, it will find the weakest of excuses, so from our perspective, we need to continue to say what we need to say in order to protect our national security."

The report follows an amendment to the Outer Space and High-altitude Activities Act, which Parliament hurried through last July, requiring registration for ground-based space infrastructure.

Also today, The Detail talks to Jason Young, the director of the New Zealand Contemporary Chinese Research Centre at the Victoria University of Wellington - he's an expert in Chinese politics and international relations.

He says the language in the SIS report was very general about the various risks New Zealanders face, but some of the case studies point specifically to China.

"There is a balance between acknowledging that the risk is not purely from one country, and also wanting to protect our diplomatic interests and trading interests," he says. "At the same time, I think it's important that New Zealanders are aware of where particular risks may come from."

Young says, given our burgeoning tech and space industries, which inherently have dual uses when it comes to defence and security, New Zealand businesses must do their due diligence to ensure risks don't eventuate. They should still act on their commercial interests, but be aware of what's going on.

"There's really no excuses, considering the information that's been put out over the last decade from the New Zealand agencies about the types of the things that they need to do in terms of managing risks."

Young says it's important also to focus on developing productive relationships with countries like China.

"I always like to say, when I'm talking about the more sensitive and challenging areas of the relationship with China, that it's always important to put in the perspective that, yes, we have these issues and these challenges, but when you look at the relationship as a whole, there's a whole bunch of really good news stories, there's a very important trade relationship, there's very strong institutionalised diplomatic links with China.

"Which is not saying to dismiss the issues and the challenges, but rather to put it in the perspective of a very complicated and significant and important relationship for New Zealand to manage."

World.title: Hawke's Bay Coffin Club searches for new home amid struggles to meet demand
World.content:
The Hawke's Bay Coffin Club donates hundreds of baby coffins to hospitals every year, but can't keep up with demand, because the group doesn't have a permanent space of its own.

The club is run entirely by volunteers and anyone can become a member, which then means they can buy and design their own personalised coffin.

The group of about 40 members are mostly elderly and retired, and gather every Tuesday morning at an old sports building in Hastings to make coffins.

However, a growing part of the charity's work is in making baby coffins, funded through the adult coffin purchases. In the past financial year, volunteers have made and donated more than 500 baby coffins, valued at more than $175,000.

"That's a huge amount for our little club and it just shows the need that is out there in society," said club treasurer Cherie Hames.

From talking to hospitals, she believes their club is the only group in New Zealand making this many baby coffins, but despite hospitals and birthing units needing more, they aren't able to meet that demand.

"We are at a point where we don't have the room to make any more," Hames said. "We are basically at capacity of what we can make on the premises, we have to find new premises."

Volunteer Pete Wolstenholme holding one of the baby coffins, which contain a hand-knitted blanket and teddy bear made by local ladies. RNZ/Alexa Cook

The baby coffins are stored in a little room out the back of the main workshop, and inside each coffin lies a hand-knitted cuddly bear and blanket crafted by local ladies.

"It's devastating," said volunteer Alan Monk. "You can imagine a family expecting a newborn and, all of a sudden, it's all over.

"That's the last thing, the absolute last thing on the list that they would have even considered they had to get ready."

The baby coffins are currently being made next to the club's main workshop, in an old cold netball ablution block, where rusty cobweb-covered showerheads still stick out of the concrete walls.

Don Mardle oversees the production of hundreds of baby coffins. RNZ/Alexa Cook

Volunteer Don Mardle oversees the operation, which he said could produce more coffins, if they had a larger building and more volunteers.

"We're restricted by space and labour," he said. "This year, we are up to 147 as of today and that's only scratching the surface really.

"I'm a retired tradie, I came here to make adult coffins, but found my space making baby coffins."

Mardle volunteers more than 20 hours a week of labour to ensure enough baby coffins are made.

"It's an incredible privilege to be doing this," he said. "I love giving to our community and, if there are any tradies out there - joiners, cabinet makers - we'd love some help," he said.

Hames said people volunteer from all walks of life and for all sorts of reasons.

"Some of the women have had miscarriages in the past and the way that was dealt with was not the nicest, so for them, it fills a real need," he said.

"On the other side of it too, we have people that are in resthomes that are still useful. Just because you go into a rest home, doesn't mean there isn't an area you can fill.

"I don't think volunteering and usefulness stops at a certain age."

Dave Beal gluing together the lid for a baby coffin. RNZ/Alexa Cook

For the past 11 years, the Coffin Club has leased its buildings off the Hastings District Council on a six-month rolling contract.

The council told RNZ the area had not been earmarked for any particular activity or development to date.

"Decisions on its future will be made by council in consultation with the community, once strategic planning work being undertaken for Windsor Park, including Splash Planet, is completed and as resources allow," a spokesperson said.

"Given that the future of the green space is undecided, council will not approve new buildings on it."

The council said any club or organisation wishing to establish premises on council-owned land may submit an application, and it had not received an application from the Coffin Club.

Hames said the club was worried it would have to move, once a decision was made about the future of Windsor Park, so the group was hunting for land in Hastings to build a permanent home and continue the club's legacy.

"We need to be somewhere we can expand and build, or alter to fit our purposes.

"Anybody willing to help donate and get us to our goal, we would really appreciate that. We are a worthwhile cause."

Hawke's Bay Coffin Club Treasurer is worried about the charity's future and hoping they can find some land and funding to continue building coffins. RNZ/Alexa Cook

'We have a lot of fun here'

Volunteer Pete Wolstenholme joined the club more than three years ago, although he's yet to make his own coffin.

"When I retired, I needed something to do," he said. "I saw it advertised and thought, 'That sounds different, I'll go down and have a look'.

"I had the thought that probably a lot of people have, that it's a bit morbid, but it's far from it. We have a lot of fun here, we're always laughing."

Pete's friend, Alan Monk, has also volunteered for several years, helping many people design their final resting place. He said Kiwis attitude toward death was evolving.

"More and more, there is an acceptance that I've got to get ready for that day, it's going to come sometime, so I've got to help my family by putting things together.

"People sort of say, 'Well, that's my final bed', so we talk about this as 'underground furniture'," Monk said.

For some, it's an opportunity to have a bit of fun decorating their coffin. Wolstenholme and Monk laugh, as they remember one member who turned his coffin into a truck.

"He was a heavy truck driver and his coffin had big lights on the front, it had a sound-effect motor in it and lights actually working," Monk said.

The friends enjoyed the camaraderie that came with being part of the club and the sense of purpose in giving back, which Hames said was a common feeling among members.

World.title: Changes for how endometriosis is diagnosed could be 'a big win'
World.content:
Changes on the way for how endometriosis is diagnosed offer hope for those living with the painful condition, Endometriosis NZ chief executive Tanya Cooke said.

New clinical guidelines announced on Tuesday will mean general practitioners can make a diagnosis based on symptoms and examination, rather than waiting for a laparoscopy.

The change puts a greater reliance on imaging, rather than surgery, Cooke said.

"So people who are suffering from the condition will receive a diagnosis much earlier and can commence treatment and this should make a big difference."

The average wait for diagnosis is currently nearly 10 years, and patients live with significant pain, she said.

Endometriosis is an inflammatory disease where tissue similar to the lining of the uterus grows outside it. Symptoms include period and pelvic pain, subfertility and infertility.

"You cannot underestimate what people go through when they're experiencing these debilitating symptoms. Young girls have to take time off school, maybe can't take on the careers that they wanted to," Cooke said.

"It can have a huge impact on somebody's quality of life. So there's hope that we can get on top of the diagnosis early and really improve the outcomes for the minimum of 120,000 people that are living with endometriosis here in New Zealand."

She said the change is "a big win" for those living with the condition.

"It's been an accumulation of sustained advocacy from our organisation, but we're excited to have international clinical best practice implemented here in New Zealand."

The gold standard for diagnosis has been surgery, which the new guidelines move away from towards updates in imaging, such as transvaginal ultrasounds and potentially MRIs, Cooke said.

Announcing the changes on Tuesday, Health Minister Simeon Brown said once a clinical diagnosis is made, GPs will then be able to prescribe treatment immediately,

The change would mean low impact hormonal medication could be prescribed without delay, which Brown said was effective for up to 60 percent of patients.

Laparoscopic surgery would remain available for those who needed it, but it would no longer be the only route to diagnosis.

Health NZ will adapt the Australian Living Evidence Guideline on Endometriosis for use in New Zealand, in collaboration with the Royal Australian and NZ College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists, other medical colleges and Endometriosis NZ.

World.title: Sydney Swans say players 'in serious breach' of club standards
World.content:
The Sydney Swans say the players allegedly connected to an incident at a Melbourne hotel "are in serious breach of expected club behaviour and standards".

The ABC understands four players — Isaac Heeney, Chad Warner, James Jordon and Riley Bice — are linked to an investigation into an alleged assault at the Pullman Hotel in east Melbourne in the early hours of yesterday morning.

It is not suggested that any of the four players are being accused of sexual assault.

Victoria Police is investigating, stating this morning that "the exact circumstances are yet to be established and … no one has been arrested or formally interviewed at this time".

The club said it interviewed all the players linked to the incident in Melbourne and concluded "firm action" should be taken relating to the breaching of club standards.

(Clockwise from top left) James Jordon, Chad Warner, Riley Bice and Isaac Heeney are understood to be linked to a sexual assault investigation. (ABC News/Getty Images)

"The club also acknowledges that these serious allegations impact others and their wellbeing must be paramount," a statement read.

"The Sydney Swans condemn all forms of abuse and disrespectful behaviour towards women. Any conduct that causes offence or harm to others is unacceptable and falls well short of our expectations. All women deserve to be respected and feel safe.

"We also want to acknowledge that the care and welfare of our AFLW athletes and staff is of the utmost importance to us as a club.

"They have been and will continue to be offered the support they require, and we acknowledge the impact these allegations have on our female athletes, staff members and the wider community."

Heeney, Warner, Bice and Jordon did not appear at Swans HQ with the rest of their team today and were interviewed by the club off-site with lawyers present.

The Swans board will meet tonight to agree on club-imposed sanctions and penalties.

Focus should not be on 'football consequences' AFLW star turned broadcaster Kate McCarthy calls out members of the media focusing on how a police investigation linked to Sydney Swans players could affect the team's finals chances.

"Any further sanctions or decisions regarding the outcome of the police investigation would take place after that process is completed," the statement read.

"During this time, we will provide the appropriate support to the players involved in the incident, along with their partners and families.

"The Sydney Swans hold all players and staff at the club to high standards of behaviour and personal conduct. Representing this club carries significant responsibilities both on and off the field, and we expect those standards to be upheld at all times.

"Our focus remains on cooperating fully with the AFL and authorities, maintaining the integrity of the process, and upholding the high standards expected of everyone who represents this club."

'Deeply concerning' incident: AFL CEO

AFL chief executive Andrew Dillon said the allegations around the Swans were "deeply concerning", stressing that, regardless of the outcome of the police investigation, the incident raised wider concerns around the game.

"The conduct and serious allegations regarding Sydney Swans players are deeply concerning," he said in a statement.

Andrew Dillon said the effects on a club's season had no bearing on the seriousness of the allegations. (Getty Images: Mark Kolbe)

"While the matter remains under police investigation, it raises broader issues for our game and our responsibilities as a sport.

"The woman who made the report to police is entitled to privacy and care, and that should be respected.

"It is important that the police process is allowed to run its course."

Dillon alluded to discussions around the potential sanctions or distractions for the Swans and the potential impact that may have on the second-placed club heading into the AFL finals.

"Sexual assault allegations are serious, regardless of who is involved, what time of year it is, or what they may mean for a season," he said ahead of the team's final home-and-away game on Sunday.

"Our first question should not be what this means for a football club. It should be whether our actions match the standards we stand for and the community expects of us.

"As a sport, and as an industry, we are clear about the standards we expect and the values we stand for and the need to uphold them.

"Being clear about our standards also means being prepared to act when those standards are not met.

"Notwithstanding the ongoing police investigation, the AFL and the Sydney Swans will consider the broader conduct of the players as more information comes to light."

World.title: Focus should not be on 'football consequences' for Swans, ex-AFLW star says
World.content:
Former AFL Women's star Kate McCarthy has questioned the tone of some of the media coverage around an ongoing police investigation involving Sydney Swans players.

Four Swans players — Isaac Heeney, Chad Warner, James Jordon and Riley Bice — are understood to be linked to a Victoria Police investigation regarding an alleged sexual assault at the hotel where the team was staying on Sunday night.

"The exact circumstances are yet to be established and the investigation into the incident remains ongoing," Victoria Police said.

"Police spoke to a number of people at the hotel, however no-one has been arrested or formally interviewed at this time."

News of the allegations yesterday sent shock waves through the league, naturally filling the slates of news bulletins and AFL panel shows.

On Channel Seven's Agenda Setters, former Port Adelaide star Kane Cornes spoke from "the football point of view" of the issue, saying the players' lack of consideration for their teammates "is what makes [him] so angry".

(Clockwise from top left) James Jordon, Riley Bice, Chad Warner and Isaac Heeney. (ABC News/ Getty Images)

"This is where I get really angry from a football point of view," he said.

"When you're two weeks away from a finals series, when Dane Rampe has played in four losing grand finals and he's probably in bed at age 36 or at home right now going, 'This is my last chance, I'm 36, I had a chance to finish second and host another home final, give myself one last chance at winning a premiership'.

"[Jake] Lloyd's played in four losing grand finals, Heeney himself has played in three. … You'd think it would mean a bit more to Isaac Heeney ... on the eve of a finals series and put your teammates and your team in jeopardy."

Loading Instagram content

On Fox Footy, Melbourne great Garry Lyon said he did not want to "understate or downplay the seriousness of" the case, insisting he could "only really comment on the one side and that is football-related matters".

"The rest will sort themselves out and again, that's not to dismiss all parties involved in this, so let's get that on the table," he said.

"What we can discuss is the ramifications from a football point of view and this is an unmitigated disaster for the Sydney Swans and for the game.

"Those pictures on the eve of the AFL finals series with plain clothes [police] and police cars outside a hotel room one week out from the finals series is an absolute disaster."

McCarthy, now a commentator for Seven and Triple M, said focusing on "the football consequences" for the team caused by any potential sanctions or distractions sent the wrong message, particularly to girls and women.

Kate McCarthy says the focus should not be on "the football consequences" of the police investigation. (Getty Images: Hancock)

The former Lion, Saint and Hawk also took issue with Swans chief executive Matthew Pavlich saying the club was "extremely shocked and disappointed that this has taken place and that the players have found themselves in this situation".

"AFL players occupy positions of enormous influence. We celebrate them as role models when they do wonderful things in the community, we can't suddenly decide they're 'just footballers' when difficult questions about behaviour, attitudes towards women and culture arise," she wrote on Instagram.

"Language matters too. Players don't simply 'find themselves in situations'. Adults have agency and make choices. Whatever this investigation ultimately determines, our language shouldn't inadvertently remove that agency or responsibility."

Current GWS player and McCarthy's former AFLW teammate, Tilly Lucas-Rodd, praised the post, while Lion star Jade Ellenger commented: "This is what using a platform for change looks like, so well said."

Loading...

The news about the Swans emerged two weeks after former AFL player-agent Ralph Carr was revealed as the "well-connected man" convicted of rape last month.

In the wake of that revelation, former player and Australian Football Hall of Fame member Sam Newman questioned the evidence in the case and said the victim "might have buyer's remorse".

McCarthy questioned how much the AFL was doing to truly engage and include women and girls in footy spaces if someone like Newman remained in the hall of fame.

"We should be asking serious questions about what and who we continue to celebrate as a league," she wrote.

"The AFL says it wants women and girls to feel that football belongs to them. That has to mean more than having an AFLW competition or getting women through the gates. It means examining the culture around men in football, how women are spoken about and treated, and how our industry responds when serious allegations involving women arise.

"This isn't about declaring anyone guilty. That is for police and the courts. When women are potentially harmed, why are we so quick to focus on what it means for the men on the football field?"

World.title: Why Tallis Duncan could be the answer for Australia's World Cup shortage
World.content:
The South Sydney backline might be an unusual place to find the answer to Australia's second-row shortage for this year's World Cup but regardless of position the form of Rabbitohs tyro Tallis Duncan is fast becoming impossible to deny.

Of the backrowers who played in this year's Origin series only Liam Martin can be considered an automatic selection for Kevin Walters's squad.

Hudson Young and Dylan Lucas are both out with injuries, Haumole Olakau'atu will represent Tonga, Briton Nikora is already tied to New Zealand and Angus Crichton's status is uncertain amid his impending move to rugby.

Duncan has improved out of sight in the past 12 months. (Getty Images: Mark Metcalfe )

Duncan would have to beat out the likes of Canterbury's Jacob Preston and Warriors veteran Kurt Capewell, and Kulikefu Finefeuiaki, David Fifita and Heilum Luki will all be in the mix if they don't opt to represent Tonga and Samoa respectively, but the door is open for him to claim his first taste of higher honours.

The 24-year old has been a rare constant for South Sydney in a helter-skelter season, impressing at second row and in recent weeks at centre.

His effort against Canterbury last week, where Duncan scored a try, threw the final pass for another and ran for 182 metres from 23 carries, has become typical fare and with the Rabbitohs hitting form at just the right time, a strong finish to the season could well propel Duncan into a green and gold jersey.

Blues bash brothers unleash the beautiful crazy Liam Martin and Hudson Young don't like to point fingers unless it comes time to decide which of the New South Wales backrowers is madder.

"It's definitely something I've dreamed about my whole life. I haven't spoken about it too much publicly, that's not really the type I am," Duncan said.

"But that's a dream and if I was able to achieve that dream it would mean everything to me and my family. That's all I have to say about it now."

Injuries have forced Duncan to spend the last month at centre and while he's still just filling in out wide, that versatility would make him all the more valuable as part of Australia's squad.

That time out wide is only temporary but his success there is proof of Duncan's growing maturity.

He's improved out of sight compared to this time last year by leaning on the experience of players like Jack Wighton and the injured Latrell Mitchell, who have both played centre for New South Wales and Australia.

"I'm a second-rower, but being able to help the team in any way, I'll always put my hand up for that," Duncan said.

"I want to be part of an environment that's team first and for me to want that I have to live that. I believe we're doing that now.

"I've got a lot of good centres around me at training and I'm not too proud to ask for help."

Duncan also believes an increase in trust between himself, South Sydney's ageless wonder Cody Walker and Alex Johnston, who Duncan cites as key to identifying opposition shapes, as a key to his recent success.

The Rabbitohs have hit form at just the right time. (Getty Images: Darrian Traynor )

At the time of writing he has as many tries this season as the Dolphins' Herbie Farnworth, the best centre in the league, and he's first in the league among backrowers for line breaks and second for tackle busts.

"I try to have intent in what I do and I pride myself on running hard lines," Duncan said.

"I know how hard it is to defend someone when they're running genuine leads, it just puts the defence under pressure.

"Everyone has a job to do and if I do mine then I'll get the ball because we've got quality ball-players like Cody and Duff (Matt Dufty)."

If the Rabbitohs' showing against Canterbury is anything to go by, Duncan will get more than a few chances to push his claims for an Australian jersey.

Wayne Bennett's side produced their best performance of the season to all but secure their top eight spot with a series of try-saving efforts the highlight of the 22-6 victory.

"I'm really proud of that one. We saved three tries before we scored one, that's what the good teams do," Duncan said.

"We might not seem like a team that prides themselves on defence but that's what we've been working on, so it's good to see the fruits of it.

"Good teams don't make errors in their own half, but when they do they defend them. We can be very proud of that."

World.title: Weatherald dropped from Test squad after stunning loss to Bangladesh
World.content:
Opening batter Jake Weatherald has been dropped from Australia's Test squad after the side's historic loss to Bangladesh in Darwin.

Matt Renshaw has been called into the 13-player squad for the second Test at Great Barrier Reef Stadium in Mackay, which begins on Saturday.

Weatherald made 23 and a third-ball duck in Australia's stunning nine-wicket loss to Bangladesh.

Shock loss to Bangladesh reveals Aussie cracks On paper, Australia's full-strength team should have wiped the floor with Bangladesh. But a lack of application to their Test match craft has left Australia vulnerable to teams that are driven to succeed in the longest format.

The Darwin-born top-order batter made his debut during last summer's Ashes series against England.

He averages 20.36 from his 12 innings in Test cricket, with a highest score of 72.

Renshaw, 30, now firms as Travis Head's opening partner for the second Test.

Renshaw played 11 Tests between 2016 and 2018, before being dropped from the side.

He was recalled to the side in 2023, when he played three Tests.

Renshaw has a highest Test score of 184, which he scored against Pakistan at the SCG in 2017.

Under-fire Marnus Labuschagne has kept his spot in the squad despite struggling for form in recent times.

Labuschagne scored 1 and 31 in his two innings in Darwin, and has not scored a century in his previous 22 Tests, averaging 25.23 in that time.

Coach Andrew McDonald said after the first-Test loss the changes to his technique had held up well, but warned Labuschagne "needs big runs".

He was not so complimentary of Weatherald.

"There was some change to Jake in terms of where he lined up and his movement patterns," the coach said.

"It's always hard to critique small sample sizes on whether it holds up. He dragged one on and drove at one in the first innings and was dismissed.

"It is probably harder with that smaller sample size to say, 'yep, that's going to hold up under pressure'."

Australia squad: Pat Cummins (c), Scott Boland, Alex Carey, Cameron Green, Josh Hazlewood, Travis Head, Josh Inglis, Marnus Labuschagne, Nathan Lyon, Matthew Renshaw, Steve Smith, Mitchell Starc, Beau Webster

Bangladesh squad: Najmul Hossain Shanto (c), Mehidy Hasan Miraz (vc), Soumya Sarkar, Shadman Islam, Tanzid Hasan Tamim, Mominul Haque Showrab, Mushfiqur Rahim, Litton Das, Amite Hasan, Jaker Ali Anik, Taijul Islam, Taskin Ahmed, Hasan Mahmud, Syed Khaled Ahmed, Ebadot Hossain Chowdhury, Musfik Hasan, Litton Das, Shoriful Islam

The ABC of SPORT Sports content to make you think... or allow you not to. A newsletter delivered each Saturday.

ABC/AAP

World.title: De Minaur advances to final 16 at Cincinnati in US Open warm-up event
World.content:
Alex de Minaur has seen off the rain and top-ranked Brit Arthur Fery to continue his campaign at the US Open warm-up event in Cincinnati.

The match was subject to three delays as the weather continued to play havoc with the schedule on Monday, but the fifth-seeded Australian overcame the disruptions to win 7-5, 7-6 (7-3) in two hours and 22 minutes.

Fery, who shot into the world's top 50 after reaching the Wimbledon semifinals at the All England Club as a wildcard, was playing his first match since Alexander Zverev ended that improbable run.

That catapulted the 24-year-old up the rankings to number 36 in the world, earning him a main draw second-round entry for the first time at an ATP 1000 Masters.

It nearly ended there at the Ohio tournament as another Australian, James Duckworth, put up a real fight before finally succumbing 6-4 2-6 7-6 (7-4).

De Minaur represented an even sterner challenge, though he was out of sorts early on, perhaps unsettled by an early rain break in his first service game, and had to save three break points in his next service game.

The match steadied until the 11th game when the world No.8 pounced, forcing a break point which he won with a firm drive that Fery returned into the net.

De Minaur then held to love to take the set, when the rain returned.

Upon resumption, the Aussie broke twice for a 5-1 lead before crumbling trying to serve it out, and the contest was tied at 5-5.

But the 'Demon' got it done in the tiebreaker to set up a last-16 showdown with either ninth-seeded Czech Jiri Lehecka or 21st seed Arthur Fils of France.

"I'm happy with the way I found a way. It got tough at the end, probably a little bit harder than it should have been," said de Minaur, who last reached the fourth round in Cincinnati in 2019.

"I played a very good match until the last rain delay, and then I had to dig deep. I had to kind of reset and take it one point at a time.

"I take confidence out of these types of tough wins, and hopefully every day I feel better and play better."

Compatriot Rinky Hijikata will not be joining de Minaur in round four after he was beaten 6-3, 6-4 by 14th seed Jakub Mensik.

Earlier, Rafael Jodar, Flavio Cobolli and Novak Djokovic's conqueror Thiago Agustin Tirante all won.

AAP with wires

World.title: Fraser named Carlton coach after leading Blues' AFL revival
World.content:
Carlton chief executive Graham Wright insists Josh Fraser's presentation alone would have been enough to guarantee his appointment as senior coach.

After a fairytale rise from 1-8 when Michael Voss exited as coach, Fraser was the unanimous choice to steer the Blues forward.

The former Collingwood and Gold Coast ruckman has won 10 of 13 games to guide Carlton into the most unlikely of finals appearances.

Sunday's draw against the Western Bulldogs sealed Carlton's spot in the top 10, with the club's board meeting to finalise Fraser's appointment on Monday.

Loading Instagram content

The results gave him the edge on untried assistants Jaymie Graham (Fremantle), Corey Enright (St Kilda) and James Kelly (Geelong), who all loomed strongly and presented to the coaching panel before Fraser did.

"Even if you removed the last 14 weeks, on his presentation alone Josh would have been the successful candidate," Wright said.

"Having run all candidates through a thorough and detailed process, for Josh to have emerged as the stand-out candidate speaks volumes of not only his credentials as a coach, but also the qualities he brings as a leader.

"He is a respectful whole-of-club leader who fosters a professional and united environment, with everyone contributing to our collective pursuit of excellence."

Even though he spent the majority of his playing career at the Magpies, Fraser's coaching journey has been largely at the old enemy.

The 44-year-old has had two stints as an assistant coach at Carlton, while also leading the club's VFL team.

When becoming interim coach, Fraser immediately ruled himself out of contention to stay in the role next year as a way to take pressure off the club.

"I have always had ambitions to be a senior coach and what the last three months have done is give me the absolute belief that I am ready, and most importantly ready for this exact opportunity, to be senior coach of the Carlton football club," Fraser said.

"When I was told that I had been appointed as senior coach, that sense of appreciation and responsibility I felt in that moment will never be lost on me.

"I firmly believe I am a product of amazing people around me.

"The collective commitment to each other and to get better every day in order to improve our football club is a privilege to be part of, and rest assured we want to continue to raise the standards in that regard."

AAP

World.title: Rugby league State of Origin heads to New Zealand for first time
World.content:
Australian rugby league's showpiece event will head across the Tasman for the first time, with the men's State of Origin confirmed for Auckland next year.

The Australian Rugby League Commission (ARLC) announced on Tuesday that Game II of the 2027 series will be played at Auckland's Eden Park.

It will be only the second time State of Origin has been played outside Australia, with California hosting a match in 1987 at Veterans Memorial Stadium, which was won by the Blues 30–18.

ARLC chairman Peter V'landys said the Origin match, scheduled for June 16, 2027, will be part of a wider rugby league festival in New Zealand's largest city.

"State of Origin is truly unique. It creates an atmosphere unlike anything else in Australian sport — fierce rivalry, raw passion and an intensity that can only be understood by experiencing it firsthand. It's a bucket-list event," Mr V'landys said.

"It's not just the Origin match fans can look forward to — we are planning a week of rugby league festivities in the lead-up to the event, starting with a Warriors game at Eden Park on the Sunday afternoon prior to the Origin fixture.

"It's going to be a complete takeover of Auckland, showcasing the best of our game to New Zealanders and fans travelling from all over the world."

Despite being a contest between Queensland and New South Wales, the State of Origin series has garnered widespread interest since its inception in 1980.

Eligibility rules were changed this year to allow some players to represent Queensland or New South Wales, but then be selected for New Zealand and England in the Test area.

Kalyn Ponga, Addin Fonua-Blake and Briton Nikora all played in this year's Origin series and will be available for Kiwi selection at this year's World Cup.

World.title: Maroons' search for new Origin coach suffers double setback
World.content:
Billy Slater's old pair of assistants in Matt Ballin and Ben Te'o loom as the two leading candidates to take over as Queensland coach, after Cameron Smith and Kevin Walters ruled themselves out of the race.

In a seismic Monday night for Maroons State of Origin officials, Smith first pulled out of the running.

The champion hooker had been the early frontrunner to replace Slater, who had publicly backed him to do a "fantastic job" if handed the job.

Billy Slater to step down as Maroons' head coach The 43-year-old, who oversaw five State or Origin series with Queensland, says he will not stay in the role for 2027.

Queensland captain Cameron Munster and Wayne Bennett had also endorsed Smith as the man to take over, before the 43-year-old ruled himself out of the role.

A little over 24 hours later, the state's most-capped player said it was not the time for him to take on a head-coaching role at the Maroons.

"I've heard comments from Wayne Bennett [endorsing me] and I really appreciate the sentiments, but it's not the role for me at this current time," Smith said on Nine's 100% Footy.

"I was lucky enough to be involved in the camp with the players and Billy when he started in 2022 and '23 and thoroughly enjoyed my time.

"But there was a reason I stepped away after 2023. I couldn't fully commit to the role and at the time that was an assistant coach, not head coach.

"And nothing in my life has changed."

There had also been conjecture that Walters could stand down from his post as Australia's Test coach after the World Cup and return to the Maroons.

Walters coached Queensland to two series wins during his stint in charge between 2016 and 2019 and would have had arguably the best resume of all candidates.

But he too confirmed to News Corp last night he would not be taking on the Maroons job, vowing to honour his two-year deal as Kangaroos coach.

That leaves Queensland officials with a search for Slater's replacement.

Ballin now shapes as a likely frontrunner, having served as Slater's assistant since 2023.

Matt Ballin is considered to be an option for the Maroons to be the next coach. (Getty Images: Albert Perez)

The 42-year-old played an Origin for the Maroons in 2010 and was a leading option for the full-time job at Manly this year before Kieran Foran's hot start.

He has been on Brisbane's staff since 2021, and is highly regarded in Queensland.

Te'o has also served as an assistant to Slater and had held a similar role to Ballin on Brisbane's staff before his high-profile exit earlier this year.

The back-rower played seven games for Queensland between 2012 and 2014, and was in charge of the Broncos' defence through last year's premiership run.

Slater's other key member of staff, Johnathan Thurston, has already ruled himself out of the running.

Josh Hannay is another who long served on the Maroons coaching staff, but it is understood Gold Coast would be unlikely to allow him to juggle Titans and Queensland duties.

Anthony Seibold has also spent time as a Maroons assistant and could shape as another option.

AAP
